Mr. WALTER iSCOTT (West Assiniboia). Before the Orders of the Day are called, I will crave the indulgence of the House in order to bring to the attention of the government a serious subject, which is outlined in a telegraphic message I have just received from the village of Davidson, in the Northwest Territories. The message is as follows :
No seed grain here, railway seem unable to help us, cannot yoh do something to relieve situation, if no seed here soon a lot of people will suffer, answer.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Davidson, I may explain, is the centre of a new settlement on the Prince Albert Railway, which runs between Regina and Prince Albert, and unfortunately the village is situated north of the point where a serious break has occurred in the railway line. I am led to believe that about five miles of the railway track, where it crosses the Qu'Appelle valley at Lumsden, is at present, and has been for some days, under water. The greater number of the settlers at Davidson are men wiho went in there only last year. They prepared their land for the crop last season, and this is their first seeding season. Consequently they have to import their seed grain, and now, just at the time when they expected to receive their grain, the railway service has broken down. This, of course, emphasizes the great disadvantage at which any community is placed which is entirely dependent on a single line of railway. That is the situation in which the people of this community find themselves, and I infer that the same conditions are existing in several of the other new settlements along that line of railway. The people in most of the settlements between Lumsden and Saskatoon went into that country. only last season. This is a very serious
give us government ownership of railways, this road particularly, because it would then compete successfully with one of these other roads, of which my friend liere (Mr. t>sl&i4 is oneTjnUe great ooudhblders or-directors. We want to build that road and hel]) the

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: matter. This is a problem which, if it is to be solved at all, must be solved immediately, because, if two or three weeks go by, the seeding season will have gone by. Of course, the solution largely depends on the efforts of the railway company. I am bound to say that, as far as I have been able to ascertain, the Canadian Pacific Railway, under the circumstances existing at Lumsden, have been doing their utmost to overcome the obstacles. It may be suggested, however, that if the seed cannot be got from the south it may be procured, through the efforts of the immigration officials-joined with those of the railway company, north of the South Saskatchewan. speakeroldname: Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I only received a moment before I came into the House an intimation that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) had received the telegram which he has read to us and I have not therefore had any opportunity of consulting with my colleagues in regard to the matter. I fancy we will all realize that in conjunction with the efforts we are making to settle that country we ought to take such steps as are necessary to prevent any undue misfortune or event such as the failure to secure seed which would result in the efforts of these settlers being rendered entirely abortive for a whole year. I think I can safely say to my hon. friend, that, although, as I have said, I have not had time to consult my colleagues upon the subject, we will take whatever steps are necessary to see that seed grain is transported and placed within reach of these settlers.

DETENTION OF STEAMER GAUSS AT BREMEN.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called I would like to call the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to a statement which appears in the morning papers respecting the dilemma or plight in which Captain Bernier finds himself in Bremen. The statement which I find in the ' Citizen ' of this morning is to the following effect :-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Germans won't let the Captain sail with the ' Gauss.'
Montreal, April 28.-A special cable to ' La Presse ' from Bremen says that the German government has refused to allow Captain Bernier to leave the port of Bremen with the steamer ' Gauss ' because $5,000 of the purchase money remains unpaid. Lord Strathcona paid $70,000, holding back $5,000 until the vessel's speed should be tested in Canada. The despatch adds that upon being notified of the situation the Canadian Minister of Marine replied that the government would stick to the conditions of the sale. The German government on the other hand, demands full payment before the vessel leaves port.
I would like to ask the right hon. Prime Minister if he has any statement to make to the House and if the information contained in that cablegram is well authenticated.
Rt. hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). There was some difference between the Canadian government and German government in respect to the $5,000, but I do not think that for $5,000 the bargain will be lost. I have not heard recently about the matter and therefore I assume the difference has been adjusted.

Notwithstanding anything contained in the thirteenth and twenty-ninth paragraphs of the said contract, the company shall, when it shall have completed the construction of the said western division in accordance with the terms of the said contract as hereby amended, and shall have supplied rolling stock to the amount of fifteen million dollars ($15,000,000), if the eastern division shall not then have been constructed and completed by the government, be entitled to the return of the deposit made under the twelfth paragraph of the said contract, or any part thereof which may then remain unforfeited in the hands of the government under the terms of the said contract ; and the company shall also be entitled to have the guarantee of the government endorsed upon the said bonds issued in respect of the western division, pursuant to paragraph twenty-nine of the said contract ; and if it is shown to the satisfaction of the government that the western division will be completed and rolling stock to the said amount of fiftten million dollars ($15,000,000) supplied before the construction and completion of the eastern division and that the application of the said deposit w'ill enable the company to so complete the western division and supply

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, before taking up this clause I want to say that I have considered the amendment suggested by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) yesterday and I think that to adopt it would improve the particular section to which the amendment is offered. Therefore, I propose to move the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We will take it up when we come to section 2 of the Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I would like the Minister of Justice to explain to us somewhat briefly, the effect of this change,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps it would be better to first explain the terms of the original contract, and then see how far the changes modify it. By the original contract government undertakes to construct the eastern^ diYjjipuI.Upoi). such loca-tion~and upon such plans and specifications, as it shall determine (Paragraph 5 of the original contract). Under paragraph 8 of the original contract, the construction is to be commenced as soon as plans and surveys are made and locations determined, i and it is to be completed with all reasonable despatch. There is no time limit in the contract with respect to the construction of the eastern division as there is with respect to the construction of the western division. The western division must be completed under the contract as amended, by the first day of December, 1911. The company however is obliged to make a deposit of $5,000,000, which under paragraph 13 of the contract-the paragraph with reference to the deposit is paragraph 12-which under paragraph 13 of the contract is to be returned on the completion of the construction of the western division by the company, and when the equipment of the whole line of railway, including of course the eastern division is provided. Now, under paragraph 22, the first equipment is to be of the value of at least $20,000,000, of which $5,000,000 is to be assigned to the eastern division.

The aid to be given to the company is to be in the form of a guarantee in principal and interest, of a certain proportion of the company's bond issue ; and bonds can only be issued when the western division is constructed and equipped, and the eastern division is also provided with its first equipment. The effect of these provisions is : that the company must complete and equip the western division and equip the whole line within the time limit fixed; whereas the government is not limited as to time for the construction of the eastern division, and notwithstanding, if there is any delay- which there will not be in the construction of the eastern division-the company would not strictly speaking be entitled to a return of the deposit or to a guarantee of the bonds until the eastern extension is completed. Of course, if the eastern extension is finished at the same time as the western, then the original agreement remains intact. I would like to put that in another form, briefly. Under the contract, as we have it, the government must commence the construction of the eastern division at once, but there is no time limit within which it is to be finished. With respect to the western division there is a time limit within which it is to be finished, and that time limit, under the amended contract, is December, 1911. The company is obliged to make a deposit of $5,000,000, which deposit when made (as it is made now) can only be withdrawn after the western division is finished, and also, after the equipment is provided not only for the western division, but also for the eastern division ; and the aid which the company is to receive in connection with the construction of the western division is in the form of a guarantee that is to be given to the company on the bonds to be issued by them, only after the western division is completed in its entirety and the equipment is supplied by them for the western and eastern divisions. Therefore my hon. friend will see, that the company is in this position :	that while they
may have complied with the conditions of the contract with respect to the western extension ; if the eastern extension is not completed at that time, and as a result the equipment for the eastern extension is not provided; then and in that event, they cannot ask for either the withdrawal of the deposit or the guarantee of the bonds. The object of the amendment is to provide that if the western extension is completed before the eastern extension-which as I said a moment ago is a contingency not likely to happen-and if the company have supplied equipment to the extent of $15,000,000 instead of $20,000,000; that is to say, an equipment which in our judgment will be sufficient for the operation of the western division, and of that equipment to the value of $15,000,000, they have ear-marked equipment to the extent of $5,000,000 which is to be assigned to the eastern extension ; in Mr. FITZPATRICK.
that event, they will be entitled to the withdrawal of their deposit and, also to the guarantee of the bonds.
Notwithstanding that the eastern extension is not completed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
And only $15,000,000 worth has been provided ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And only $15,000,000 worth of rolling stock has been provided. Of course, the whole reason for the amendment is :	that possibly under the
contract; there being no obligation on the government to construct within the time limit fixed with respect to the western extension ; the eastern extension might not be ready at the same time. That is the whole reason of the amendment. Of course, the criticism of my hon. friends will be, that it is not seriously intended to proceed with this eastern extension, and that this amendment is intended for the purpose of enabling the Grand Trunk Pacific to have their line complete from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean, and when they have supplied the equipment for that section they will be entitled to the return of the deposit which we held, and they will then be under no obligation to provide the equipment for the eastern division. The answer to that is, that if the eastern division is completed within the time limit fixed for the construction of the western division, of course the contract in its original form remains intact ; the obligation to supply $20,000,000 of rolling stock remains, and also, when the eastern division is finished, if the western division is finished at an earlier period, the obligation to supplement the rolling stock so as to provide us with $20,000,000 worth remains absolutely also.
The deposit goes in the meantime ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The deposit goes in the meantime.
They get that money back ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They get that money back. I repeat: instead of our having that deposit as security to us for the equipment of the whole line, if the eastern end is not ready at the same time as the western end, then, in that event, the $5,000,000 goes, and we have only $15,000,000 of equipment.
Is not the net result of the amendment to relieve the company from the provision of $5,000,000 of rolling stock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are relieved of the obligation to supply the additional $5,000,000 of rolling stock until such time as the eastern extension is completed, if it is not completed at the same time as the western extension. The obligation to provide $20,000,000 of rolling stock remains intact; but the security which results from the deposit of

$5,000,000 disappears if they succeed in completing the western extension before we have completed our eastern extension.

X do not see any objection
whatever to the change made by this clause. I think the arrangement proposed here might well have been put into the original contract. The only difficulty I see is this, that in the event of a contingency arising by which the $5,000,000 deposit is to be returned, the country thereafter will have to rely for the provision of the final $5,000,000 of rolling stock simply on the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think I made that point clear. The obligation to provide this $5,000,000 remains, except that instead of forming a part of the $20,000,000, it forms part of the $15,000,000.
I understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The 22nd paragraph of the original contract provides among other things for equipment to the extent of $20,000,000. of which $5,000,000 is to be marked and assigned to the eastern division.

That is perfectly clear. I understand the clause precisely as the Minister of Justice has explained it ; but I still point out that after the $5,000,000 of rolling stock has been appropriated to the eastern division, there will be only $10.000,000 for the western division instead of $15,000,000. In that case all the government have to compel the provision of the final $5,000,000 for the western division is the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. They will not have the security of the original deposit, which was contemplated to ensure that that would be done. I do not mean to say that is a thing that should stand in the way of the agreement ; but I do think that some security might have been provided that that would be done, such as a deposit of some of this capital stock. But, so far as I am concerned, I do not raise any objection to the clause as it stands.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is just this to be said about it-that, assuming, as we have to assume in all these contracts, the possibility of a breach by the other party, the government might find themselves face to face with this proposition. The $5,000,000 of rolling stock might not be provided, and then what remedy would the government have ? It would not be of much use for them to bring an action against the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, because its assets would be covered by first and second charges. After all, it seems like leaving the matter very much to the discretion of the company, so far as the equipment of $15,000,000 for the western division is concerned. I would like to ask the Minister of Justice what will be the practical working out of the scheme provided for marking the $5,000,000 of rolling stock ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This, I suppose, is a question of railway management rather than of law ; but I apprehend that for the purpose of identification, this stock to the extent of $5,000,000 can be marked as having been assigned to the eastern division. I do not know what the practice in general is, but I do know that when plant is leased, the lessor of the rolling stock has the opportunity of marking it in such a way as to identify it.
This will not interfere with the use of that rolling stock on any part of the railway ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Then, I do not see that it makes any difference whether it is marked for the eastern division or for the general use of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The eastern division is to be operated by the company under a lease. The condition is that they shall equip that division with rolling stock to the extent of $5,000,000, to be marked for the purpose of identification, so that we may know that that is the quantity of rolling stock assigned to that particular division. With respect to their obligations under the lease, that rolling stock will be secured to us as part of the equipment of that eastern extension ; and if the company fail in the performance of the lease, and we take the eastern division over, the rolling stock so marked will of course go with the eastern division, and form part of the equipment.

Is there any provision for the rolling stock in case the eastern division is not finished for years after the western division ? The rolling stock may be used on any part of the railway, and what provision is made that it shall be as good as when first bought ? If the company have the privilege of using it on any part of the road, it may be worn out and consequently of very little value at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provision with respect to that in the original agreement is that they must have equipment which is modern and first class. That agreement will be read as speaking at the time the company carry out their obligations under it. Their obligation, at the time the extension is handed over to them, to be operated under their lease, will be to furnish complete rolling stock, modern and in first class condition at that time.

I do not like to differ from the Minister of Justice, but I would think that the time would be when the rolling stock was set apart; and if the government allowed it to be used, they might be out, so far as the security is concerned, to the extent of whatever depreciation would have taken place in the stock while in use.

With reference to this rolling stock assigned to the eastern division being in first-class order, there is this provision in the 22nd clause of the original contract:
And the first equipment for the completed road shall be of the value of, at least, $20,000,000, of which not less than $5,000,000 worth shall be supplied for the operation of the eastern division of the said railway, and the said $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock, together with all renewals thereof and additions thereto, shall be marked as assigned to the said eastern division.
I would like to ask the minister whether there is any other provision regarding the rolling stock than the one I have just read. This clause speaks of renewals, but it is not provided in specific terms that the $5,000,000 of stock shall be kept up to its original condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The concluding words of that paragraph will have some effect as regards the construction to be put on it:
And the said $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock, together with all renewals thereof aqd additions thereto, shall be marked as assigned to the said eastern division and shall be held to be and form part of the equipment of the eastern division of the railway during the said period of fifty years, and shall be used as the equipment appertaining thereto, according to the ordinary practice of railways during the said period of fifty years.
Would not that imply that the obligation of the company is to maintain that equipment in an efficient condition according to the ordinary practice of railways ? Then you have the next clause, clause 23, which provides :
\ The lease of the said eastern division shall contain all necessary and proper provisions required by the government for securing, during the entire term of the said lease, the efficient maintenance and operation of the said division, including all repairs and renewals, and the maintenance and renewal of its rolling stock and equipment, so as to keep the said division, in all respects, up to the standard of modern and efficient railway practice ' and operation, as the same shall be advanced and improved from time to time, during the whole term of the said lease.

With reference to the clause which the hon. minister has just read, I am afraid that hardly meets the point. That deals with the question of base, but I am speaking of a case in which there may not be any lease, namely, where the western section is completed before the eastern, or possibly before the eastern is begun. In that case there will be no lease of the eastern section actually executed and no provision for the keeping up of the rolling stock to its original standard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree upon that point.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
That point, I think, is worthy of being considered. With regard to the part of section 22, to which the minister was good enough to refer me, that is the part providing that the $5,000,000 of rolling stock shall be held :
To be and form part of the equipment of the eastern division of the railway during the said period of fifty years and shall be used as the equipment appertaining thereto, according to the ordinary practice of railways during the said period of fifty years.
I do not see that that strengthens the position. I would be inclined to think that that provision was rather for the protection of the company. We have heard a good deal about the company leasing rolling stock, and I assume-I think it is quite capable of that construction-that this concluding part of the section is for the purpose of enabling the company to comply with the terms of the contract without actually purchasing the stock. It would ' enable them to lease the rolling stock, according to the ordinary practice of railways, during the period of fifty years.' More than that, it is probably intended to cover this case which no doubt will arise under this contract. The rolling stock is interchangeable between the eastern and the western divisions, and it may be sent east and west over the whole line, as it may be required, from time to time, * according to the ordinary practice of railways, during the said fifty years ; ' and I think there is, even with the reference which the minister has been good enough to give me, a good deal of question as to whether that rolling stock, if it be not required for use on the eastern division, will have to be Kept up to the state of efficiency in which it was at the time it was new. If those provisions are not such as the minister suggests they may be, if they have not the effects he suggests, we may have this state of things. We may have stock, which is ear-marked for the purpose of complying with this provision, used in connection with the western division, and depreciated in value not only by user, but by reason of the fact that at the time the eastern division is completed it will be out of date.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Linder the original contract, the obligation of the company would be to equip the eastern extension with rolling stock of a modern and efficient character. My hon. friend will admit that 1
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In what respect does my hon. friend think the amendment is a departure from that obligation ? We must not forget that except where it is affected by the amendments, the original contract remains in its entirety. It is quite true that the $5,000,000 rolling stock forming part of the $15,000,000, will be

operated in connection with the western extension during all the period that may elapse before the eastern extension is completed, and of course during that period there will be user and depreciation ; but when they come to equip the eastern extension, they must do it according to the lease. The lease then takes effect, and the obligation which they have incurred to supply proper rolling stock will apply, and it will be the duty of the government to see that this stock is in such a condition as the contract stipulates it must be when the lease is made.

Th^s could be got over if the Minister of .Tustice could define when the $5,000,000 of rolling stock is to be given in security for the eastern division. The company have to provide that rolling stock before they can withdraw the $5,000,000 deposit. Of course, they will use that stock. You do not expect that the government will insist that it should be laid aside and not used.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course not.

The whole question then is, when will that rolling stock be taken ? It does seem to me that it will be taken when they are allowed to withdraw their deposit. Consequently there will have to be another arrangement, and the government will have to decide whether it will insist on the company making good the depreciation wh'ich may be caused the rolling stock by the use of it.

I wish to refer to what the Minister of Justice said immediately preceding the remarks of my hon. friend. I am not prepared to dispute his statement that when the time comes for actually equipping the eastern division, the rolling stock must be equal to the requirements of the original agreement. We must look at all these matters. I presume, in the same way as they would be looked at in a court of justice having regard to the general scope of the contract But what I would direct the attention of the hon. gentleman to is this- that, although it may be perfectly true, as he says, that, when the time comes that the company has to actually equip the eastern division for use, then, although the lease will compel them in words to comply with the original provision for five millions of dollars worth of rolling stock, yet, we have only the covenant of the company. The security is gone; we plart with our security when we obtain rolling stock ear-marked for the eastern division to the value of $5,000.000. Then, when the time arrives, three or four years afterwards, when it becomes a matter of immediate necessity to equip the eastern division, we have the covenant and liability of the Grand Trunk Pacific to make up stock for the eastern division to the amount and value of $5,000,000, but we 731
have no security deposited for the purpose of that contract, and we have to depend on their liability under the original and amended contract and whatever lease they may enter into.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot pretend to say that our security for the equipment of r\ the eastern division is not to be decreased \ by the release of the deposit. It would be ( absurd to say so. I admit quite freely that, 1 to that extent we decrease our security. I \ am not here to say that black is white and i white is no colour at all. But the contingency for which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) seeks to provide is a contingency which cannot possibly arise. It is not conceivable, in view of the assurances that have been given, the undertakings that have been entered into and the interests that exist in this country, that the eastern section should not be completed to Moncton at the same time with, if not sooner than, the western division. I cannot conceive that as possible in view of the absolute assurances given to this House and the country. I cannot conceive it possible, in view of the fact that the , whole policy of this scheme falls to the I ground if we have not the eastern extension I to enable the Grand Trunk Railway to com- j municate with the west. And I say, further, [DOT] that it is impossible to conceive that the i Grand Trunk would have a western division * extending from Winnipeg to the Pacific < ocean and no connection with their Ontario system. It is impossible to conceive that. Then, if the extension is built for a thousand miles through northern Ontario to connect with the Grand Trunk system at North Bay, there is no government in this country that could disregard that fact. It may be that, when this contract is to be given effect to, this government may have shared the fate of other governments and passed away. But, once the road is constructed for a thousand miles through northern Ontario it will be impossible, in view of the conditions existing then, for any government to abandon the extension of that line to Quebec and Moncton.

I agree with the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that probably nothing will be gained on this side by discussing this clause. But it seems not out of place to point out that in the change now being made the government is acting consistently with what they have done in every clause of the original and amended contract. The Minister of Justice has pointed out that'in this case there was an oversight in the original contract, which oversight operated not against the country but against the Grand Trunk ; and the Grand Trunk came to the government and pointed out that, in case of the government not completing the eastern division as soon as the western division was completed, hardship to the Grand Trunk would result. And

the government were clearly justified, when this was pointed out to them, in remedying the hardship as much as they could. But 1 wish to point out that, by the course they take, the government remedy the hardship in such a way that the security given to the country for the performance of the work is lessened by about $5,000,000, if the view of the ownership of the equipment taken by the Minister of Justice is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no use trying to avoid that.
So, again the government failed to safeguard the interests of the people, even though the favour asked was entirely in the interest of the Grand Trunk.

I would like to have placed distinctly on record-probably with the concurrence of the Minister-the effect of the alterations made. There is one view of the matter which the hon. minister, I think, did not refer to. I understand the Minister of Justice to have referred to every change that has been made by this amendment in in a very candid way, and in a very fair way, with the exception of one. There is one that I would like to refer to, to see if I understand it correctly. And that is in the concluding part of main section No. 2 of tlit supplemental agreement:
And the company shall also be entitled to have the guarantee of the government endorsed upon the said bonds issued in respect of the western division.
That is introductory. This follows which. I think, is an alteration in the contract which has not been referred to :
-and if it is shown to the satisfaction of the government that the western division will be completed and rolling stock to the said amount of fifteen million dollars ($15,000,000) supplied before the construction and completion of the eastern division, and that the application of the said deposit will enable the company to so complete the western division and supply rolling stock to the said amount, and that the same will be so supplied, the said deposit shall be released by the government in such instalments as may from time to time be agreed upon.
Now. I understand that this is on the same line as the original agreement and merely varies it in amount. So, we have this state of things to keep in mind-I am not discussing now, whether it is a good or a bad state of things-that without complying with the original or any agreement, without building the western division, the company may, if it is made to appear to the government that tney will complete the western division and will supply the rolling stock under the original and amended agreement, obtain the release of the security.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I do not think so. Would my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) Mr. NORTHRTJP.
be good enough to look at section 13 of the original agreement ? I understand this to mean that when the western road is practically completed, and the equipment of $15,000,000 supplied, if it is shown to the satisfaction of the government that the $5,000,000 on deposit, if applied to the completion of the construction or the purchase of rolling stock, will complete that construction and supply the equipment, then it may be released in such instalments as the government may determine. But it is only on condition that the result will be to get the western extension completed and the $15,000,000 of rolling stock provided.
I suppose this will be as good a time as any to ask the minister whether there will be a clause added providing that rolling stock is to be free from any lien.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The matter was discussed last year and we considered that the question was absolutely free from doubt, under the terms of the contract. I may say it was in the mind of everybody at the time tile contract was made, that the rolling stock should be the absolute property of the company. It was discussed at the time, the parties to the agreement had it in their minds, and the agreement was drafted for the purpose of making that absolutely sure.
I now say. and I say it deliberately in the presence of the Prime Minister and on behalf of the government, that the rolling stock is to be supplied to the satisfaction of the government, and that it is the deliberate intention of the government to say that no rolling stock can be supplied to the satisfaction of the government, unless it is rolling stock which is absolutely free from all encumbrances, so that under the terms of the contract, we shall have a first charge upon it.

I presume, that being the case, the minister will add a few lines to the clause, because the Grand Trunk have given the government notice in the most deliberate manner that they intend to secure (hat rolling stock through a trust company. There is evidently no misunderstanding between the directors of the Grand Trunk Company and the government, and certainly as I read [DOT] the contract, from a Canadian standpoint, I think it is quite open to the Grand Trunk Pacific to provide that rolling stock on a trust lease. It is evidently the intention of the Grand Trunk to do that, because they have deliberately notified and stated in a public meeting of their shareholders that this is how they intend to raise the money to secure that. Surely the government, having that notification of the attitude of the company from the general manager of the Grand Trunk, to the meeting of the shareholders, that they intend to obtain that rolling stock by raising money and giving the

229S
rolling stock as security-surely the government will not think it too much to take precautions so that there shall not be a' misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My recollection of the meeting at London, is that the general manager did not use quite the terms now referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Osier).
I have here the official report of the proceedings containing, as I am informed, all that took place and issued by the company.. I quote the following from the words used by the president at the foot of page 33.
He boldly states that the liability upon the Grand Trunk will amount to 9,000,000 pounds sterling,

This is referring to Mr. Allen.
-and he divides that 9 millions sterling into 3 millions liability in respect of guarantees, 5 millions in respect of rolling stock, and 1 million in respect of the deposit. As regards the 3 millions in respect of guarantees, that, as I stated to you will undoubtedly be a liability. As regards the 5 millions for rolling stock-in the first place, the estimate is not 5 millions, but 3 millions. With that the Grand Trunk Company has nothing to do. That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and, as the general manager will perhaps tell you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund.
These are the words used. I want to further state that I have read carefully over what Mr. Hays is reported to have said, and I And that he makes no reference to that at all :	he does not implement the
statement of the president. I would like to say that, as I read these words, there is nothing absolutely contradictory in the positions taken by tlie president of the Grand Trunk and by myself. They may provide this rolling stock by the aid of a trust fund, that is utterly immaterial to us. It is perfectly immaterial how they raise the funds to provide the rolling stock. What is material is that they should give us that rolling stock under such a title as would enable us to have a first claim upon it, to the exclusion of all others. That is what the contract calls for and what we will insist on.

Is it not a simple matter to make that quite clear, because no one familiar with railway matters can misunderstand the reference to a trust company. It is the common, ordinary way of raising money by all the leading railways ; there is hardly a leading railway on this continent or in England in which the same thing does not prevail, the rolling stock is raised through a trust fund, and is earmarked to identify it, and under the contract which is made by the builders or vendors of , the railway stock with the company, the payments are extended for from five to fifteen years, and until the last payment is made, the title of that rolling
stock remains in the vendor. This is not open to discussion ; any one familiar with railway matters knows what the Grand Trunk president means when he said that.
I quite believe that lit is the intention of tlie government to l|ave the rolling stock placed upon the road without a lien upon it, but surely when the government have been notified, deliberately and clearly, of the intention of the Grand Trunk, they should make it so clear that it will not be open to dispute hereafter. Why not put a very simple line or two in this agreement, making it quite clear that the rolling stock is to be put on the road without a lien ?
The rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and as the general manager will tell you they have laid their plans to provide the rolling stock by a trust fund.
This is practically the same as the wording of the report from which the hon. gentleman has been reading ; this is from the verbatim report of the Grand Trunk shareholders. There is not any question.
I think, that the Grand Trunk Pacific people intend to raise the money for that rolling stock by giving a lien upon it, and if there is no clear definition of that put in the present contract, we will next year have the Grand Trunk Pacific coming to this parliament and stating that they understood that they were to be permitted to provide that by a trust fund and* are unable to raise that $15,000,000 in any other way. There will be no other way for them to raise it except in this way, because they will have no other credit left; they will have exhausted every credit and every asset they have, there will not be a credit remaining to them when this contract goes through, on which to raise $15,000,000 or $500,000, ana we will have the exhibition of these gentlement coming back next year and saying they are not able to raise $15,000,000 and asking the government to consent to their raising it through a trust fund. Is it not the part of ordinary common sense to so define this, that there can be no dispute, and if the Grand Trunk people say that they cannot raise this money except by a trust fund, let us deal with it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This matter was the subject of an interesting discussion last year. I then expressed the opinion of the government with respect to the construction we put upon this contract. I also read to the House, the opinion of the counsel who were engaged to draft this agreement, and I also quoted the opinion of the deputy Minister of Justice who was consulted in connection with it. All this took place last year when this contract was going through. That was sufficient notice to the Grand Trunk of the position this government intended to take, and of the construction which they intended to put upon this contract. Since that time the matter! has

been discussed by the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway and has been the subject of an amended agreement, but it never occurred to them, notwithstanding the discussion, notwithstanding the knowledge they had of the position the government was going to take, to ask for an amendment, to ask for any change. It has never occurred to them to bring the question up. Why should we make trouble for ourselves ? We hold that this contract is complete, that its terms are fully expressed and if my hon. friend will bear with me for a minute, I will give him in a few words the reason why I hold the opinion. The eleventh clause of the contract provides that :
The company shall lay out, construct and equip the said western division, &c.
That is the first clause in which the word ' equip ' is found. Then comes section 12, which provides that the company are to make a deposit of $5,000,000 :
' As security for the construction of the western division and for the first equipment of the whole line of railway.
Then section 13 provides that the deposit put up for the purpose of securing the construction of the western division and the equipment of the road may be returned to them in instalments, which instalments are to be used for the purchase of the equipment. Then, if you go on to section 19, you there find that:
For the purpose of enabling the government to determine the cost of construction of the said railway, or of any portion thereof, or the cost of the equipment supplied.
Does that imply a lease ? We have a right to make an examination into their accounts, so as to be sure that the cost of the equipment is up to the value that they are called upon to provide. That is $20,000,000. If we are entitled to investigate the cost of the equipment, does that imply that we shall investigate the title under a lease ? In section 22 it is provided that:
The company shall equip both divisions of the said line of railway with modern and complete rolling stock suitable and amply sufficient for efficient operation and the handling of all classes of traffic to the satisfaction of the government

Here are the words that are important:
-and the first equipment for the completed road shall be of the value of, at least, twenty million dollars.
.First we have the right to investigate the cost, and then we provide that the value of the equipment shall be $20,000,000. Then, in clause 23

Jj. BORDEN. Will the hon. Minister of Justice permit me to ask him a question before leaving that, because I have not been quite able to follow his argument, or1 Mr. FITZPATRICK.
rather to agree with him in regard to this question ? Does he mean that the word ' equip ' implies absolute title, or that the word ' value,' used in the context, 'would imply absolute title? What I suggest is this: Suppose that one's house should be said to be furnished with furniture costing $5,000, or that I should undertake that a certain house should be furnished with furniture of that value, would there be necessarily any implication as to the title ? I should think not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Undoubtedly not. I think the hon. gentleman is perfectly right. I never argued that the obligation to equip implied the obligation to give a title, but I say that when we read this contract we have to read all the sections together, and read them in such a way as to give effect to every line and every word of every section. Section 23 provides that:
The lease of the said eastern division shall contain all necessary and proper provisions required by the government for securing, during the entire term of the said lease, the efficient maintenance and operation of the said division, including all repairs and renewals and the maintenance and renewal of its rolling stock and equipment.
Is it to be a lease for fifty years that they are to give us of this rolling stock ? Could they give us leased rolling stock, would that comply with the terms of that condition Then, we have much more than that. Section 34 provides that:
Inasmuch as the bonds to be guaranteed by the government only make provision for a part of the cost of construction of the western division, the company hereby agrees that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall guarantee bonds of the company for the balance required for the construction of the said western division-
These are the words that are of importance.
-exclusive of the said twenty million dollars required for the first equipment.
They are obliged to guarantee the bonds of the company necessary to build the road, exclusive of the cost of equipment. Does that imply a lease ? Would the leasing of rolling stock comply with the terms of that section ? Then, after all, you get back to section 35, which is one of the most important clauses in the whole contract, and in which clause it is provided that:
For the purposes hereinafter in this paragraph respectively defined, the company may and shall create mortgages to trustees, as follows
(a) A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property.
If this rolling stock is held under lease, under which lease, of course, the title remains vested, until the performance of the conditions, in the lessor, how can they give

to us upon that equipment a mortgage which Shall be a first charge ? Do not the words ' first charge ' imply a charge which excludes any other charge, or any charge in the shape of a lease, or of any other character ? Then the words of section 37, in respect to the purchase of material, are as follows :
The company shall purchase all material and supplies required for the construction of the western division and the equipment of the whole of the said line of railway from Canadian producers.
There is an obligation to purchase this equipment from Canadian producers. I do not lay emphasis at the present time upon the purchase from Canadian producers, but on the fact that they are obliged to purchase this equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to argue the question any further, but in view of the statement made by an hon. gentleman of the prominence in business circles of the hon. member for West Toronto, I am obliged to reply that it is not the view of our government, and that it is certainly, as far as the government are concerned, not their intention, and I do not think that any person, by any construction, will be able to so interpret this agreement.

One must not forget that while the construction put upon this agreement by the government is in some sense important, the construction, after all, if there is to be a difference between the Grand Trunk and the government, will be niade by the courts, and it is the courts
which will decide. Governments come and go. Even if this government should be in power, it would not have the construction of this agreement left in its own hands, and it the government says that it means one thing and the president of the Grand Trunk says that he thinks it means another thing, it is for the courts to decide really what it does mean. It does seem to me that when last year the government was expressing so strongly its belief in the construction it now adheres to, when hon. gentlemen take a different view, and when legal opinions are obtained from outside the House, as good legal opinions can be obtained in the country, supporting the view held by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, some attention should be paid by the government to the arguments which have been advanced in opposition to the view which it takes of the contract. Surely, in no ordinary private transaction would any solicitor or counsel dare to advise his client to run the risk of insisting on an interpretation that he thought was right when so many eminent counsel held a different view.
The Minister of Justice told us to-day that he read the opinions of certain legal gentlemen last year. I do not at the moment remember how their opinions were worded, but I do know that the Minister of the Interior, in his speech of this year, professes to have the opinion of Mr. Shep-ley, of Toronto ; a gentleman whose opinion always carries weight, and which no doubt is a very interesting and valuable contribution, but which has no more reference to the point we are discussing and were discussing then, than the flowers that bloom in the spring. I would call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that the only point in the clause is the word ' equip.' If ' equip ' implies purchase there is not the slightest doubt but that the Minister of Justice is correct; if equip does not imply purchase, then the portion of the clause he read has no reference to the subject at all. The Minister of Justice did not read clause 15, and I submit that one cannot come to a reasonable interpretation of the word ' equipment ' without reading that clause. Amongst .other items, clause 15 provides for the rental paid for the rolling stock rented for the use of the eastern division. When one finds in this document itself, a provision made for the rental of the rolling stock to toe charged up in that way ; would it not be idle to contend that there was no intention to have any of the rolling stock leased. Clause 35 which refers to the mortgage, does not bind the company to own any rolling stock of any kind. Unless there is something in the Act, outside of the mortgage clause to compel them to purchase rolling stock, there is nothing to compel them in the mortgage clause, which merely says, that they have to give security on all the property they own. If they

do not own property they cannot give security on it. If they do purchase any rolling stock, that would be included under this clause and would be put in the mortgage, but unless there is a clause somewhere else which requires them to become owners of the rolling stock, there is nothing to lead to any other conclusion than that which I contend for. As to clause 37, with regard to the purchase of material in Canada ; we all know that that was put in, in order to secure protection to Canadian manufacturers and producers, but that does not state what the company is required to purchase. I submit that in view of the difference of opinion which exists amongst legal gentlemen in this House, and amongst eminent counsel outside of this House, and in view of the fact that we"have had the opinion of eminent counsel in support of our views, and in view of the fact further, that the president of the Grand Trunk Railway holds the same view that we took in the House last year ; surely there can be no possible objection to the Minister of Justice putting in a clause, defining the meaning of the word * equipment ' and making it clear beyond peradventure. If the president of the Grand Trunk misunderstood the clause, no harm can be done ; and on the other hand if the Minister of Justice is wrong (and to err is human) then at an early stage of the proceedings we will save protracted and expensive litigation, by inserting a few words to define what the word ' equipment ' means in this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course lawyers will differ even if they do happen to be on opposite sides and one is interested in criticising a contract and the other in maintaining it. My hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) said that Mr. Shepley's opinion had not very much to do with the question, and I think in referring to it he broke out into poetry about the flowers that bloom in the spring. Let me read the opinion of Mr. Shepley, given on the 8th of April, 1904 :
On the 14th August last you wired me as follows :-
Examine provisions agreement between government and Grand Trunk Pacific and say whether provisions of agreement with regard to equipment of the railway would be fulfilled if company should supply rolling stock not owned but leased or hired by them for that purpose. Examine paragraphs 22 and 33 A. I was not in Toronto at the time, but at St. Catharines, and my firm repeated the message to me there. On the same day I wired you from St. Catharines as follows :-Examination of clauses 11, 12, 13, 19, 22, 23, 35 A and 35 C, as published ' Globe ' 31st. July and 1st August in my opinion not be fulfilment of contract by company. On the following day I wrote you from St. Catharines a letter of which the following is a copy :-
Tour telegram was repeated to me here yesterday afternoon and after a long search I found a copy of the ' Globe ' containing the Mr. NORTHRUP.
contract between His Majesty and the representatives of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Co. I telephoned a wire from here to Toronto, which I suppose was duly sent on to you last night.
To-day my firm has sent forward your letter with the inclosures. ' After further consideration, I am confirmed in the opinion expressed in my telegram of last night. I do not see how in view of the provisions in the contract tc which my telegram refers, it is possible to argue that a leasing or hiring of rolling stock would be an 'equipment' within the meaning of the contract. It is manifestly intended-[DOT] and I think the intention sufficiently expressed -that the rolling stock forming the contract equipment shall be the property of the company in such sense that the first mortgage contemplated by section 35 A and the mortgage contemplated by section 35 C shall both operate upon a clear ownership vested in the company.
I may add to the sections mentioned in my telegram clause 11 of the Act of Incorporation as tending to support the view I have ventured to express.
In addition to getting the opinion of Mr. Shepley I consulted Mr. Chrysler, who confirmed Mr. Shepley's opinion and concurred in it. Then, for my own personal satisfaction (my deputy being absent at the time the contract was being drawn) I consulted Mr. Gormully, the solicitor for the Bank of Montreal, a man whose reputation so far as a matter of this sort is concerned stands second to none in this country ; he also confirmed the opinion given by Mr. Shepley. As I said last year, my own deputy, Mr. Newcombe, concurred. It will not be necessary for me to read the opinion he expressed, but let me make this short extract :
The line cannot be said to be really equipped within the meaning of the clause with rolling stock ' suitable and amply sufficient for efficient operation and the handling of all classes of traffic ' when all the title that the company has is a leasehold interest or an equity of redemption which may be terminated or foreclosed at any moment.
I' read those opinions now, simply because of the opinions expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup). I think it would be fair for my hon. friend to look at the question from the standpoint that all this was said last year before the contract was submitted for approval to the Grand Trunk shareholders at the meeting in London, and before a suggestion was made with respect to an amendment. The Grand Trunk Company have never expressed a doubt on that subject; they have never asked us for any modification of the agreement in that respect, and under these circumstances I fail to understand how it could be possible for them, to argue in good faith, that there is any doubt as to the construction to be put on this agreement.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It would seem that the attention of these gentlemen who have
AP~RIL 29, 1904
given legal opinions has not been directed to clause 14 of the original contract which is absolutely inconsistent with the opinion jest read, and I shall show how. The word ' equipment ' is apparently regarded in that opinion as indicating absolute ownership of the rolling stock which was placed upon the road, but if you look at section 14 of the contract you will see that the word ' equipment ' cannot possibly be used in that sense. I would thank the Minister of Justice to send me over that opinion, for, of course, one cannot understand it properly from just hearing it read ; I would like to read it. Clause 14 is very specific :
14. For the purposes of this agreement, the expression ' working expenditure,' as applied to the eastern division of the railway, shall mean and include all expenses of maintenance of the said division, and of the stations, buildings, works and conveniences belonging thereto, and of the rolling and other stock and movable plant used in the working thereof, and all such tolls, rents or annual sums as are paid in respect of property leased to, or held by, the company in respect of the said eastern division (apart from the rent of any other leased line), or in respect of the hire of rolling stock let to the company as part of the equipment of the said eastern division, &c.
If that does not imply that, in some circumstances and under certain conditions, the equipment of the eastern division shall be hired, and not absolutely owned, I do not understand the meaning of the English language.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My expectation was that we should have this question out before this measure was through. I have no objection to letting it stand. We can have it out again.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I could not gather much from the opinion of Mr. Shepley quoted by the Minister of the Interior. It seemed to be an opinion that was telegraphed, as words were omitted which made it almost impossible to follow it unless one had before him the case that was submitted to Mr. Shepley. The further opinion which lias been submitted by the Minister of Justice to-day is a written opinion, and of course it will be easy to gather from it what Mr. Shepley's view is. So far as any criticism of these opinions is concerned, if I venture to criticise them, I will defer it, because one thing on which I agree with the Minister of Justice is that it is not desirable to give off-hand opinions upon a statute or upon considered opinions given by counsel. I would say with regard to the last opinion that clause 14 of the Act could hardly have been before the learned gentleman who gave it, although a perusal of the whole opinion may alter my opinion with regard to that. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has not of course forgotten the very full argument that was made on this point by the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), who dealt with the question of working expenses in this connection, although from a somewhat different standpoint and with a somewhat different purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 14 has not escaped my notice, and I am quite certain that in the course of my conference with Mr. Shepley it did not escape his notice, although possibly he does not refer to it. So the equipment of this part of the road to the extent of $5,000,000 the title must be absolutely in the company ; but any other part of the equipment they may bold under any title they please. Our security is limited to the extent of $5,000,000. and it is only with respect to that that I asked the question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If I were to give an opinion along the lines given by these learned gentlemen, for whose opinions I have every possible respect, one of the first things I would have dealt with would have been section 14.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Shepley himself drew the contract for the government.

Then, naturally he would back up his own contract. What a grand opening this affords for a good lawsuit. Although the matter could be cleared up by the insertion of two lines, tlie Minister of Justice deliberately leaves it open to a fat lawsuit. Does it not seem absurd not to make the matter perfectly straight and plain by putting in a few words when we have the power to do it ?

Referring again to the alternative amendment of section 13 of the original contract, the Minister of Justice pointed out that, as be understood the contract, this only applies in case $5,000,000 will complete the equipment of the road. I was addressing myself to that branch of the case, both in reference to the consideration of this clause, and for the purpose of calling attention to the fact that this gives the company very great latitude. Although the construction put upon clause 13 of the original contract by the Minister of Justice may be perfectly plain in the way be states, it is not equally plain in the clause that is now introduced in amendment to that. Section 13 of the original contract says :
Provided, however, that when it is shown to the satisfaction of the government that the application of the same will enable such construction and equipment to be complete.
I presume that means the application of the So.OOOJlOO. But it is unfortunate, though probably not fatal, that the same phraseology is not adapted in the amended contract; and I notice that the same system prevails in other parts of the contract. For instance, in section 1 of the amended contract a different phraseology is adopted from that employed in the original contract; and when that occurs, as the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) points out, it always

invites litigation. If the hon. minister will refer to the wording of the amendment embodying the same alternative provision, he will notice that it has not the same wording as the original section, and is not equally clear. But, assuming that the matter may work out in the way the minister says, I wish to call attention to what was said by him in his opening remarks this afternoon. We have this additional latitude allowed "to the company, along the same lines as before, and as soon as they have come to within $5,000,000 of completing their contract, and assuming that they have provided an equipment of $10,000,000, they can get all this security released. But more than that. It may happen that we shall have a deteriorated stock at the time we come to obtain the execution of the lease with reference to the eastern division. So that although the government have the right to call upon the company to equip the eastern division with $5,000,000 of rolling stock and to mark that $5,000,000 rolling stock as appropriated for the eastern division, as soon as the company obtain the release of their deposit, the company may continue to use that rolling stock on the western division until such time as the eastern division is ready for its use, and it will necessarily depreciate. That depreciation will ultimately have to be made up, and the only security we have that it will be made up is, not the security of a money deposit, but the good-will of the company. That is the legal aspect of the case. Let me say that I do not agree with my hon. friend from East Hastings that this is a reasonable concession to the company, in view of all the circumstances. I feel that it is another evidence of the fact that every concession made is in favour of the company and not one in favour of the country.

I suppose that section 2 is not considered finally adopted or approved while this question of the construction of the agreement is under consideration by the Minister of Justice. I understood him to say that he would consider the points that were being discussed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not consider the question of the rolling stock closed at all, but I expect the section to go through and when we get the contract finally through the committee, we may ask the committee to rise and have the whole matter discussed at a later stage.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3,
Pending the completion of the eastern division by the government, the company shall be entitled to lease from the commissioners, to be appointed under the said Act, and to operate such portions of the said eastern division as may from time to time be completed, but upon such terms as may be agreed upon between the Mr. LENNOX.
company and the said commissioners, which terms are not to be more onerous than those of the lease of the whole division by the said contract provided for, save in so far as may be necessary to give full effect to the paramount right of the said commissioners next hereinafter mentioned, and subject always to the paramount right of the said commissioners to use and operate the same without any payment of tolls or other compensation for such purposes as they may deem necessary or expedient in the execution of their commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 9 of the Act which provides for the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway refers to the operation of the eastern division until completed. The section reads :
The construction of the eastern division and the operation thereof until completed and leased to the company, pursuant to the provi-ions of the agreement, shall be under the charge and control of three commissioners.
The object of the amendment is to provide that pending the completion of the eastern division, and according as each section is completed, the government shall have power to lease each section to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Is the Grand Trunk Pacific bound to take over the section ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not bound, but entitled to lease it. Tinder the Act providing for the construction of the National Transcontinental Railway, you will find that the eastern extension, until completion, is to be operated by the commissioners. This is to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific to lease from the commissioners such portions of the road as are completed.
They need not lease any portion unless they please.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not until it is complete. Their obligation as to taking it over comes into effect only when it is entirely completed.

The commissioners are here given power to lease such portions of the eastern division as may from time to time be completed, pending the completion of the whole division. I think everybody will agree that the first section of the eastern division which will be completed must be that portion between Winnipeg and the junction of the North Bay branch. There are two points where junctions may be made. The line being constructed from Winnipeg-easterly, the Grand Trunk Railway will first construct for a distance of perhaps 300 miles, a branch to Lake Superior. The main line will then proceed still further easterly, until it meets a branch running down to North Bay. Everybody knows beyond doubt that that portion of the eastern division will be the first completed. In fact, it is that part that must be constructed first to make the prairie section useful to the Grand Trunk Pacific or Grand Trunk Railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How does my hon. friend know that it will be tbe first completed ?

Because it must be in order to enable tlie Grand Trunk Pacific to get at tbe prairie section. If the junction between Winnipeg and Lake Superior and the junction between Winnipeg and the North Bay branch are not completed early, there is no object in building the prairie section, because in that case the Grand Trunk Railway would have no connection with the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not go on with the line further east at the same time ?
The first section to be completed will be that which I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We do not admit that.

I assert that beyond a doubt. I do not think there is an hon. gentleman who doubts it except perhaps the Minister of Finance, and I do not admit that he doubts it. But I make that exception as he has just said that he does not admit it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) speak of branch lines ?
The line to points of juncture with branch lines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is speaking of the main government line.

I am speaking of the main government line from Winnipeg to the junction first with the Lake Superior branch and then easterly to the junction; with the North Bay branch. I say that these two sections of the government work must necessarily be completed-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps there is a misapprension. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) I understand has reference to two lines, one the branch line to Port Arthur and the other the government line from Winnipeg round to connect with North Bay.

No, the Minister of Justice has not quite understood me. The government line, called the eastern division, will proceed easterly from Lake Winnipeg towards Lake Abitibi about 300 miles easterly of Winnipeg where it will strike the branch that the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to build down to Lake Superior. Then, when it comes five or six hundred miles eastward it will strike the branch that leads to North Bay. These two branches in connection with the main line, will give the Grand Trunk just what its original idea was-a connection with Lake Superior and with its system at North Bay. Now, until that section is completed the prairie section will be almost useless to the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What will be the distance, from the point of intersection with the North Bay branch, to Toronto ?
It will be, perhaps, 370 or 400 miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nearer five hundred.

It depends, as the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) said yesterday upon where this survey is going to run the line. No doubt, the Grand Trunk will run it where it will pay the Grand Trunk best. The. government is allowing the Grand Trunk to do the surveying, and the nearer they can run the line to North Bay, the better for the Grand Trunk, but, perhaps the worse for the government. They may even run it through a very costly country in order to get the junction point as near asi possible to North Bay. But that is not what I am arguing. What I speak of is the line from Winnipeg to the point of junction with the North Bay branch. In order to get through to the east with the traffic from the prairie country no doubt that will be the first section completed. There can be no reason for completing any other section before it. And yet, this supplementary contract contemplates that one portion shall be completed before another. Now, what is the position when that section is completed ? The position is that the commissioners may lease this 800 or 900 miles of the main line, which the Grand Trunk was willing to construct itself-had applied for a charter to enable to construct as its own work

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not the Grand Trunk.

The Grand Trunk Pacific. But cveryhoilv ***<)!>ikiiif>'it a'lLlrTtffWGrand Trunk Pacific charter belonged to the Grand Trunk. They just put in the word 'Pacific ' that is all. The Grand Trunk Pacific was willing to build that portion of the work itself. Now, the government have undertaken to build it; and they give these commissioners power to lease it to the Grand Trunk until the final completion of the whole 1,900 miles to Moncton. And on what terms ? On terms that will not be more onerous than the terms for the whole eastern division when it is completed, and the terms upon which that lease is to be made are that not a cent shall be paid to the government for seven years
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) mean to say that the Grand Trunk would have built that line from North Bay without the support of tlfe government, if they had been allowed to do so ?	.
That is another question.
What is the difference?

I say that the Grand Trunk Pacific applied for a charter last

session to enable It to build from Winnipeg to North Bay. They intimated that they were going to ask for a subsidy, and I suppose they would have done so. But let me say this-if the Grand Trunk Pacific had been allowed to go on with their work under their proposed charter allowing them to build from the Pacific ocean to North Bay, they would never have expected to get such a subsidy as the government are giving in connection with this western division. Does anybody suppose that, if the Grand Trunk had been allowed to go on with the project of last year, they would have come to this parliament and expected parliament to give them seven years' interest upon the cost of construction ? No one ever heard of such a thing being sought by any company. Would they have expected the country to undertake to guarantee seventy-five per cent of the cost of construction V Has that been done in any other case ? Why, the terms granted for the western division alone would be far more than they would have expected from parliament for the whole distance to North Bay. There is no question about that. No one ever heard of such a subsidy being granted to a company that undertook such a work under the conditions of the present day. Mackenzie & Mann, or the Canadian Northern, or whatever these companies are called, did not get any such concessions. The Grand Trunk would not have expected to get from parliament the concessions they are getting under this contract ; and I say they were ready, therefore, to build that section themselves. And what is the result of it all? The commissioners may give this section over to the Grand Trunk for the time between its completion and the completion of the whole eastern division, charging them no interest or rental ; and, when the main lease comes into operation, by the very terms of this agreement, they will get the road again for seven years for nothing. Now, what I want to know is this : Why did not the government say to the Grand Trunk, when arranging thjs supplemental agreement : If you want that particular section from Winnipeg to the junction point on the line from North Bay, you must pay rent for it ? They might not only have said that, but they might have made it conditional that the Grand Trunk should take over this line and pay a reasonable interest on the cost. What does the arrangement made by the government mean ? At the lowest estimate given by bon. gentlemen on the other side, the cost of that road, irrespective of interest during construction will be $31,000 per mile. If you add interest during construction, the cost will be $34,000 to $35,000 per mile. Allowing that the road will be 900 miles long-we cannot tell exactly what the mileage is not knowing where the junction point will be, but it will be about that length-there will be something like $30,000,000 spent by Mr. BARKER.
Canada to construct that road, and the commissioners are enabled to give the Grand Trunk Pacific the lease of that property and not ask a dollar of rent for it. And yet, this portion of the road is not a property that will have no revenue. It will be that portion of the line over which all the traffic will pass from the prairie section through to Montreal and Portland. It will be the route by which all the merchandise and manufactures from the older provinces going to the west will pass to Winnipeg.
In summer.

Winter and summer

anything that goes all-rail will go that way. If there is any part of the road that will be profitable to the railway company it will be this highway by which the traffic to and from the prairie section must pass. Now, Sir, is it not preposterous to say that the country should spend $30,000,000 in constructing that and then give the commissioners power to hand it over without receiving a penny ? The country, during all the time of the completion of the road, have to provide the interest on the money borrowed. I think, Sir, it would have been the least that would have occurred to hon. gentlemen opposite to say : You shall use that when it is completed, because it is a perfect connection with your system ; we impose no hard terms upon you, but we give you the very line that you yourselves wanted to construct, we pay for the construction, we will hand it over to you for operation and you will avoid having [DOT]to find the money for that portion of the road, we say now that you shall operate it and shall pay the interest upon its cost. That would have been a perfectly fair demand for this government to have made under the circumstances, and yet it does not seem ever to have occurred to the government that anything should be asked for the use of that 800 or 900 miles of road. The only explanation I can get of it is that they really thought the commissioners could make a fair charge for its use, and that they would get something by way of rent but they possibly overlooked the fact that under the seven year clause of the lease they could not charge any rent.
