They seem to have overlooked these seven years altogether. What was the object of saying that the terms should not be more onerous than the original lease when the original lease meant no rent at all. The government thought they were to get something for it, but they overlooked the fact that under the terms of the original lease they could not charge any rent. I think that the clause requires some explanation from the Minister of Justice beyond what we have had thus far, and I would like to hear wliat it is.

I would like to know what authority the hon. member for Hamil-
. 2313

toil (Mr. Barker) has for saying that the original proposition of the Grand Trunk Pacific was to build from North Bay to Winnipeg. My impression was that their original plan, was to build from North Bay to apoint north' of Lake Nipigon and thence to the Pacific coast.
Oh, no.

That was until Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson came to Winnipeg and interviewed the Board of Trade.
Mr. BARKER, If my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) will refer to the Bill introduced by the Grand Trunk he will find there is nothing about that.

I am saying what was originally contemplated by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays. The plans produced and circulated through that country by the G. T. R. showed a line drawn north of Lake Nipigon and, north of Lake Winnipeg, but after interviewing the Board of Trade of Winnipeg and seeing that great city and its commerce, Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays concluded. it would be folly to go north of that city and changed their course. But admitting, for the sake of argument, that the original intention was to go from North Bay to Winnipeg, has my hon. friend (Mr, Barker) any license to say that the Grand Trunk would have undertaken to build that road without material assistance from the government, without as great assistance as is to-day being granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific ? We will for the sake of argument, admit that the government would give the same guarantee as they are today giving for the mountain section, i.e., guarantee 75 per cent of the cost of construction of the road from North Bay to Winnipeg. The Grand Trunk would undoubtedly have asked that much assistance. Then we would not have had running rights for the Intercolonial Railway ; that new road would have been the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific. To-day we have a road owned by the government- not by the Grand Trunk Pacific-over which the Intercolonial Railway may run, a road owned by the people and not by private corporations and any other road may also run over it. Looking at the question from an engineering standpoint no man would venture to say that a line could be built from North Bay to the head of Lake Nipigon and on to Winnipeg with as good gradients as can be obtained from Winnipeg to Quebec. I do not think an engineer in Canada would say that you could build such a road. You might as well say that you could build a railway sloping down the precipitous banks of the Ottawa river as from North Bay to Winnipeg. From an engineering point of view it is
impossible. I have spoken to men who have gone over that country and they know it is impossible. Admitting for the sake of argument that the Grand Trunk are going to connect at a point some distance north of North Bay with their Ontario system, I ask why should they do this? Suppose that their main line runs to a point 300 to 400 miles north of North Bay, then would it be cheaper for them to haul grain and produce down to North Bay and to the lakes which are closed in the winter, than to haul it from Winnipeg to Quebec ? The line from Winnipeg to Quebec will be cheaper, shorter and have a better gradient and they can haul more grain over it. It is true that western Ontario may not send products over that line ; but western Ontario is not all Canada. I was told the other day that on the largest train of goods that ever went into Winnipeg, carrying 83 cars, about a mile long, as many carloads came from points east of Toronto as from Toronto and points west. All manufactured products are not from the western part of Ontario. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) is quite mistaken in some of his premises, and I think in future discussions he should correct them. He has no license to say that the Grand Trunk has not demanded as much for the construction of the line from North Bay to Winnipeg as they are now demanding for the construction of the line through the mountains. Had the government acceded to the wishes of the Grand Trunk Railway we would have had a very much worse bargain than we have, the present arrangement secures a shorter railway, better built, and with better gradients.

The position of the hon. gentleman now seems to be simply that he is trying to excuse the government and to apologize for the enormous subsidies they are giving the Grand Trunk, by making the assertion, without any justification whatever, that the Grand Trunk would not have proceeded to carry out their original intention unless this government built the road from North Bay to Winnipeg and guaranteed three quarters of the sum required to build the prairie section and the mountain section. What justification has the hon. gentleman for saying this ?
I have the justification that they asked that very assistance.
From whom ? Unfortunately the facts are against the hon. gentleman.
Not at all.

Mr. Hays is on record on the 24th of November, 1902, and he has put himself on record since then, and so has the president of the Grand Trunk Railway. The hon. gentleman must know that, if he knows anything at all. On November 24th

last, Mr. Hays Issued a statement which was published first, I think, in the Montreal ' Star,' and afterwards in the Toronto ' Globe.' In it he said :
This company is now prepared to go right ahead with a railroad extending from North Bay or Gravenhurst on our present line through that portion of northern Ontario, familiarly known as New Ontario, through Manitoba to either Bute Inlet or Port Simpson.
The road will be of the most modern and up-to-date character for the handling of both freight and passenger business-in fact, the road will he of the highest standard in every respect.	*
No one who has been studying the *wonderful developments that have taken place in the Northwest during the past few years can fail to be deeply impressed with the growth of this extensive and rich territory ; and our directors feel that in view of the apparent need of additional railway facilities, and in order to guarantee the present Grand Trunk system direct connection with that very important and growing section of Canada, the only wise policy is to take active steps towards this extension.
We are entrenched in the central portion of Ontario, the manufacturing district ; hut when it comes, to taking goods to the west, we' only get the haul as far as North Bay. Under the circumstances, it has been felt that further development was necessary, and hence the present scheme.
That is the statement published from Mr. Hays' pen on November 24, 1902, in Montreal.
Where is there a word in that statement about building a road without a N subsidy or assistance ?

The maintenance of the position of the Grand Trunk, as Sir.Rivers-Wilson pointed out, and as Mr. Hays has since declared, impelled them to seek an entrance to the Northwest Territories. Mr. Morse who, I think, was vice-president, made a statement in Winnipeg. I said that it was last November that Mr. Hays made a declaration upon this subject. I should not have said last November, because it was on November 24, 1902, that he spoke, which is a year and a half ago. Mr. Mors' made this statement at Winnipeg :
We are going to build at once. . . What is more Important is the fact that we are not a new company. . . . Having connection through the best manufacturing districts In the east and to the Atlantic sea-board, that your people are most anxious to reach, you can see how it will benefit the west. On the one hand, is direct connection with manufactories that can supply the needs of houses in the west ; on the other is your direet line hack to the sea-board. Of course, what we look to is the magnificent opportunity of opening up and developing one of the greatest stretches of country under heaven. I refer to that boundless tract of land which lies to the northwest of you.
Now, the hon. gentleman sees the justification he has for asserting that unless the government of Canada built this road from North Bay or from north of North Bay Mr. CLARKE.
to Winnipeg, provided $13,000 a mile for building the prairie section and provided $30,000 or $40,000 a mile for building the mountain section, the Grand Trunk would not have gone into this proposition.
That is not the statement I made and not the inference that the bon. gentleman should draw from the statement I made-

I would be very sorry to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, and l will give way to him if I have made any statement misrepresenting his position. He says that the Grand Trunk Company would no1 have gone on with their proposition unless they got practically all that this government is giving them, and unless the government made them a present of a line fiom North Bay to Winnipeg, for ten years without paying anything for it, and for forty years afterwards by paying three per cent interest upon the cost, guaranteed them $13,000 a-, mile for the prairie section and guaranteed them three-quarters of the cost of the mountain section together with the payment of interest of the cost of the mountain section for ten years after it has been completed. Is that the position which the Grand Trunk Company are taking now ? or were the Grand Trunk Company only faking the people when they made the announcement, and when they said that it was essential to the continued prosperity of their company that the traffic of the west should be secured to tbe Grand Trunk Railway Company? Is that the justification hon. gentlemen are depending on for this prodigal bargain with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which they have voted shall be carried through the House as speedily as possible ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentle-n an has in his hands a statement on which he relies to make his point. Would he kindly inform the committee wherein that statement says anything to justify the statement he now makes that the Grand Trunk Railway Company intended to build that road without aid ?

The lion. Minister of .justice must be drawing upon his imagination when he says that I made the assertion that the Grand Trunk Railway Companj expected to build this road without aid. But, I defy any hon. gentleman to show that before'the Grand Trunk Railway Company made their statement as to their intention to go into the Northwest Territories, they expected, or had any guarantee, or undertaking from this government that the line from North Bay to Winnipeg, would be built and presented to them, and that they would get the enormous assistance they are getting in constructing the line through the prairies and to the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No body has ever argued anything of the sort.

The hon. gentleman for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) argues that this must be a provident contract, because the read would not have been constructed if the government had not given the Grand Trunk Railway Company aid. I repeat that every public utterance jnade by Mr. Hays, every utterance made by Mr. Morse, and every utterance made by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson demonstrates the fact that it was a matter of self preservation for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to obtain access to the west as speedily as possible, and Sir Rivers-Wilson and Mr. Hays have stated again and again_the reasons why. I heed not take up the time of the committee by repeating them. Mr. Hays pointed out that last year they had 24,000,000 bushels of grain handed over to them by roads which collected that traffic in the west, I presume, the Canadian Northern Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, that this traffic went a long way to enrich their system throughout Ontario and to give it- an enormous amount of business, but that they had no assistance or guarantee that that traffic would be continued to them, and that hence, in order that they might be able to provide dividends for their shareholders in the future, as they had done in the past, it was essential that they should gain access to the west.
By what route ?
By what route ?
By North Bay.

By the route from North Bay to Winnipeg and the route from the head of Lake Superior to Winnipeg. Mr. Ross, the other day, pointed out that the construction of the branch line from near the city of Winnipeg on the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to Port Arthur, would enable the company to develop their business over the great lakes by way of their ports on Lake Huron and the Georgian Bay in the province of Ontario. The government, by this propositiou, are doing practically for the Grand Trunk Railway Company what the Grand Trunk Company intended to do for themselves. I presume that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would have secured only the reasonable assistance usually given, of $8,200 a mile, or possibly $6,400 a mile, to have enabled them to have gone on with the work. But, even with that limited assistance, the government could have made piovision, if there was any advantage m making it, that the Intercolonial Railway should have running rights over the road which the Grand Trunk Company proposed to construct.

It seems to me that at last after the hon. gentleman's statement, we have got the opposition just where we want them. The hon. gentleman lias said during this discussion that the Grand Trunk Railway could not possibly carry grain all-rail to the seaboard.
Who said ?

That was the view of every hon. gentleman who spoke. Now the hon. gentleman says that there was handed over 24,000,000 bushels of grain to the Grand Trunk Railway Company that was collected by other roads, and that the Grand Trunk got the benefit of it.
No, the hon. gentleman must not misrepresent me.
And that the Grand Trunk were going to build a railway from North Bay, via the north of Lake Nipigon, to Winnipeg, in order to enable them to secure that traffic.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon ; I made no such statement. I have their statements here, and I repeat that Mr. Hays and Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson both declared that it was essential for the maintenance of the present condition of prosperity of the Grand Trunk Railway Company that the traffic which they now have handed over to them at their ports on the Georgian Bay and Lake Huron should be continued to them, that they had no guarantee that under the present conditions it would be continued, and that it was essential to its continuance that they should get access to the west and gather up that traffic for themselves, so as to be able to send it down by the lakes to be hauled over their system in the province of Ontario.

The hon. gentleman has not said a word about North Bay. Will not ' Hansard ' show that he said that it was necessary to build from North Bay ? Asked if it was necessary to construct that road from North Bay to Winnipeg to get that traffic of 24,000,000 bushels, he said it was.

Not at all. I am sure the hon. gentleman does not mean to misrepresent me. If the hon. gentleman knows where North Bay is, if he knows its location in the province of Ontario, he knows that the statement he attributes to me would be absurd. North Bay is not within 200 miles of the ports I am speaking about-Goderich, Midland and Sarnia. North Bay is an inland town, it is not a port at all, as the hon. gentleman knows.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word in reply to the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) as to the terms of this lease. We are advised and believe that he is entirely unwarranted in the statement that a temporary lease of any of the sections of this road which have been constructed is to be had on the terms which he states. The idea that the company are

to get a temporary lease of these sections as they are constructed and pay no rental is entirely unwarranted. However, that is a question of legal interpretation, upon which it is not fit that I should dwell. It was another point on which I wished to make an observation in reply to the hon. member for Hlamlillton. He started out, with the assumption that this section from Winnipeg to North Bay must of necessity be built first. The hon. gentleman has no warrant for that statement whatever. That section is part of the eastern division of the road extending from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Quebec to Moncton.
I did not say that it must of necessity be built first I say it will undoubtedly be built first, and I say so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Anybody hearing my hon. friend would assume that the Grand Trunk had the building of it. But I will accept his amended statement that it will undoubtedly be built first. Why should it be built first V Wherein does it occupy a different position in reference to the whole undertaking from that of any other given section ? There is no distinction. It is a part of the eastern division. That division is to be constructed by the government. I take the responsibility of saying that all sections of the road must be pressed forward, and the hon. gentleman has no right to say that the western end or that section, from North Bay junction to Winnipeg, will be built first and that the other will be built after. There is no reason why an equal number of miles eastward of that may not be built as rapidly as that section, unless there are physical difficulties in the construction of the road. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) desires to convey the impres sion that the portion of the road east is not to be vigorously prosecuted. I say, on behalf of the government, that such an impression is entirely unwarranted. The whole section from Winnipeg down to Quebec and down to Moncton is an obligation equally binding on the government. There is no one part of it which is more binding than the other ; that portion which is in the province of Ontario, and that portion which is in the province of Quebec, and that portion which is in the province of New Brunswick, they all stand as part of the same scheme, and the government would certainly make a fatal mistake if they would follow the suggestion of the hon. gentleman and construct the western portion of that first and leave the eastern portion uneon-structed. I for one am prepared to say that the eastern portion of that road must be dealt with in the same manner as the section between Winnipeg and North Bay junction.
And at the same time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And at the same time ; unquestionably, Sir. I undertake to say, that this government would be guilty of a gross Mr. FIELDING.
piece of deception to the people of northern Ontario, to the people of northern Quebec ; to the people of New Brunswick ; to the people of all the maritime provinces, if they would adopt any such policy as that which my hon. friend suggests.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The best proof that the statement of the Finance Minister is not to be regarded with a very great deal of- well, I might say ' faith,' not desiring to use an offensive term-is that up to the present time the only portion of the eastern division on, which any surveys have been made, is that portion to which my hon. friend from Hamilton referred ? If there is an intention on the part of the government to make the same progress on all portions of the line, how is it that not a single surveyor has been sent out by the government ; that surveying parties have been at work within the past six months on the line between North Bay and Winnipeg, and that these surveys are being made, not by the government but by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That is a very strong circumstance to be taken in connection with the further circumstance, that that very line was a part of the project of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the first instance. If I am not correct in my statement concerning the surveys, then the government are in a position to correct me. I am relying on the information we receive from the public press. The surveys which have been- referred to by the Minister of Interior as being made by the Grand Trunk Company have not been placed before the House, and we have not much information in regard to them. Tfiis was the original project of the Grand Trunk Company, and it is the project which as the directors of the Grand Trunk have asserted is essential to the continued earning of dividends. I quote from the Railway ' News ' of the 12th of March last, in which Mr. Hays is reported to have said to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk :
We are to-day handling from fifteen to twenty millions-last year it reached 24,000,000- bushels of grain, which came across the lake from Lake Superior down to our ports, feeding the whole Grand Trunk system throughout Ontario, and this gives us the whole of the way from Montreal, thus contributing a very large portion of our earnings. We cannot hold that to our system if we do not take some means of fastening it to us. (Hear, hear.) That business to-day, gentlemen, is given to us by our competitors.
My hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) says that very large trains of manufactured goods, one recently comprising eighty-three cars, go from the east to Winnipeg. He said that a considerable portion of that freight came from the east of Toronto, but he did not deny that a very large portion of it came from the province of Ontario, and the route for freight of that kind would undoubtedly be by this line from North Bay. In that

regard, he is presenting to the House exactly the same argument which was presented by the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway to his sharehdlders, because continuing, Mr. Hays expressed himself as follows :
The Grand Trunk Railway is in this rather ridiculous position from a business standpoint of gathering up traffic from the largest and most prosperous portion of Canada, taking it to North Bay, our connection with the Canadian Pacific, and from there giving it to the Canadian Pacific to haul across the country into this prosperous and rapidly developing district we are speaking of.
I am not saying that the Grand Trunk Railway should not have assistance to get into the North-west. Last year I expressed an opinion favourable to that proposal, subject to the qualification, that I thought certain conditions should have been imposed upon them by which public aid should not go to build up foreign ports. The manager of the Grand Trunk goes further in the line of what the hon. member (Mr. McCreary) says, and he continues :
That traffic will be lost to us if we do not tie it up, so that to-day the question is not what your position is going to be if you embark on this enterprise, but what it is going to be if you do not embark on this enterprise.
Great importance is attributed by those in charge of the interests of the Grand Trunk Railway, to their getting connection at North Bay with the west. The first point which they emphasize is, that they shall gather in the Northwest that traffic which comes to Midland, and not only have the haulage from Midland but the haulage from the points of production in the west, to Port Arthur or Fort William. They apparently regard it as equally important that they should have their own line into the Northwest, and not only gather up, but carry on their own line, the traffic which they now deliver at North Bay to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Those two things are regarded as of vital importance by them. Further on, in his speech, the general manager of the Grand Trunk said :	[DOT]
Here is the Grand Trunk, the parent company, standing with a large traffic ready to deliver it westbound. This traffic is now given to a competitor. It does not have to wait five, ten or fifteen years to build up a traffic ; it starts with a traffic right from the beginning, and that is of a most remunerative character,- a high class traffic, consisting of agricultural material, dry goods, boots and shoes, and all that class of merchandise that a new and rapidly developing country requires. The Grand Trunk as it is to-day, hauls it 200 miles and hands it over to a competitor and gets nothing back. Is that a business-like position to be in ? Is that a position for the directors and management of the Grand Trunk to maintain and to acquiesce in ? I do not think you will say so.
In view of the importance attached by the Grand Trunk to getting this connection ;

if there is any legal opinion which the government is prepared to lay before parliament showing that the view which my hon. friend takes as to the legal construction of the contract is not correct, I would be very glad to see it. Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Justice will of course deal with the legal points which have been raised ; but as to the other points which the hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Hamilton have been discussing, their argument would have much force if they had not omitted to give this important fact its fair value, that the section to which they have referred is to be built by the government of Canada, and the government of Canada have the right to determine when and how rapidly it is to be built. The assumption on the* part of my hon. friends opposite that the government will of necessity build that section before all the others is unwarranted.
It will be in the interest of the country that you should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be in the interest of the country that the whole line shall be built as rapidly as it can be-not that we shall select one part and give it the preference over another part. That policy, I undertake to say on behalf of the government, will not prevail. That may be left with the government. There is no distinction made in the contract between that section and any other section ; they are all parts of the eastern division. The government is obliged to build them all as rapidly as possible. The only thing that makes it possible that one section may be completed before another is that one may have more physical difficulties than another.
What section is that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no reason to say that of any particular section more than another ; but of course if we meet with phvsical difficulties, we shall have to observe them. That is the only part of the argument to which I care to refer. The hon. leader of the opposition sought to give force to his contention by calling attention to the fact that the surveys east of Winnipeg are being made by the Grand Trunk Company. He regards this as a very remarkable thing : he cannot understand it. That which is a mystery to my hon. friend is capable of being understood in a single moment when viewed in the right way. This legislation which the government enacted last year was given assent to by His Excellency late in the month of October. If the government had found that the Grand Trunk Company were proceeding to carry out the undertaking according to the engagement of their representatives-because, of course, the Grand Trunk Company itself, by its shareholders, had not at that time ratified it; but if the government had found no hitch in the transaction, it would have been undoubtedly their duty to have appointed the commission and proceeded at once with the surveys. not to proceed to appoint commissioners until they had the amended legislation which they are now asking from parliament. But in the meantime the Grand Trunk Company, for their own purposes, and before they had entered into this contract with the government, had begun the survey of that region at the time they had come forward with their original scheme-that which hon. gentlemen opposite want to champion and approve of in this discussion. We are willing that they should have that glory. We are willing that it shall be understood, in the words of the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup), that hon gentlemen opposite, one and all, to a man, were willing to support that scheme of the Grand Trunk people for a railway from North Bay to the Pacific coast. Whatever glory there is in that, we give it to them freely. We know that that was not the policy of this government. We propose a different policy, and my friend is willing to give us all the glory of that fact.
All the glory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman for that concession, and we mean to reap the fruits of it in the public mind. But the Grand Trunk Company, at the time they made application for a charter for their original scheme, had started out survey parties.
They were dead in earnest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And hon. gentlemen opposite, we are told, were dead in earnest in wanting to help them in that anti-Canadian policy, which they tell us is the policy of the Grand Trunk Company. The hon. gentlemen opposite have placed upon the journals of parliament a motion which declares that the Grand Trunk Company is an antiCanadian company. They have in their motion declared that the interests of the Grand Trunk are bound up with Portland. And yet they say that every man of them is prepared to support that anti-Canadian company in its anti-Canadian policy of building a line from North Bay to the Pacific coast. But, Sir, to come back to the main question, I want to say that the Grand Trunk Company, being in dead earnest in that matter, and perhaps expecting that they were going to get the support of hon. gentlemen opposite in that anti-Canadian policy, started out their survey parties. Those parties have been in the field for some time. The government have nothing to do with them. If it turns out that the survey work done by the Grand Trunk Company is adapted to the line which the government will ultimately adopt, there is no reason why these surveys should not be utilized by the government; and if they were approved by the chief engineer of the government there would be no reason why they should not be bought and paid for in the ordinary course of business. But there

is no agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk with respect to those surveys. The company started the surveys for their own purposes, the surveyors were in the field before the contract was made with them, and. the Grand Trunk Company have seen fit to keep on making them. That is the whole story. The government, finding that there was some difficulty between the company and themselves with regard to this contract, and finding it necessary to come to parliament for amended legislation, deemed it wise to obtain that legislation before appointing their commission to proceed with the work of construction.

speechtext: My hon. friend has simply emphasized what was said on this side of the House with regard to this matter. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend does not doubt that at all. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

the Grand Trunk Pacific. He did not specify exactly what kind of fruits they expected to reap. So far as the country is concerned, it does not seem likely that it will ever reap any fruit.

BORDEiN. As we are going along with these sections, I would like not to have any misunderstanding with my hon. friend the Minister of Justice about what took place between us yesterday. It is probable we shall have to move some amendments to the first section. It is clear that we cannot move amendments to the sections of the contract. The only way in which we can formally place our views on record is to move amendments to the sections of the Bill. These amendments may, as in some cases last year, have the effect of overriding the provisions of the contract. I only want to arrange so that there will be no possible misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No misunderstanding. Before the House rose for dinner we were considering a criticism offered with regard to paragraph 3 of the contract. As I understood my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), the criticism he offered was that, under the terms of the amendment, the result of the lease that would be made for the purpose of operating some of the finished sections of the eastern section would be that, with respect to these completed sections, there would be no rent payable for a period of seven years, if the company were to operate during that time. I understand his argument to be that, under the original contract, the eastern division is leased for a period of fifty years ; during that fifty years the company has to pay three per cent on the cost of construction for forty-three years, and for seven years they are to be exempt from payment of any rent or any interest and with respect to three years, if they do not pay rent, the sum is to be added to the
*2329

cost of construction, on which interest is to be paid thereafter. In answer to the hon. gentleman's statement, I may say that such a contingency as that he mentions was not in contemplation so far as any of the parties to the agreement were concerned. And I will add that, in my judgment, the difficulty does not exist. At the same time, the objection is put forward seriously, and it is certainly worthy of being considered. And, while I do not entertain any doubt on the subject at the present time, I want an opportunity to consider the matter more fully and more carefully. The leader of the opposition said, before the committee rose for recess, that we had one thing in common-we were not anxious to commit ourselves to legal opinions without having considered the points fully. Out of deference to the House, I have not expressed opinions hastily ; and, as I wish to consider this point fully, I would ask that the section be allowed to stand. I say, in all seriousness, that the objection is one that deserves consideration. I want to consider it, and to give the House my reasoned opinion, such as it is. The government, of course, always have the means of preventing the contingency to which the hon. gentleman has referred. It can exercise that power by simply not completing one section in advance of the other. An absolutely effective way to prevent it is for the government to do as they intend to do-build the whole line at the same time.

It does seem to me an extraordinary way of getting out of a difficulty arising out of an imperfect construction of a contract for the government deliberately so to perform the work that it has contracted to do that it would overcome the difficulty it has got into.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The^hon. gentleman is assuming that we admit that we are in a difficulty. That is his opinion.

It is quite necessary in order to take the position that the subject is arguable. But the Minister of Justice says that the government has control of the situation, because if it finds that it is exposed to the difficulty that I have named, it can so carry out the work as to circumvent the company with which it has entered into a solemn contract. I really do not think that this is a position that ought to be assumed by the Dominion of Canada for one moment. But, Sir, the hon. minister points out that we have entered into a contract for a lease of the main line when fully completed for fifty years, and he commences at the rear end of it and tells us that for forty years we get a rent, for three years we capitalize a rent and for seven years we get no rent. Why does not the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) commence at the other end ? For the seven years we get no rent. There is nothing on the face of this contract to
show that the line may not be still uncompleted at the end of fifty years, and then for seven years we will get no rent, for three years we will capitalize the rent and for forty years we will get 3 per cent. That is the position this unfortunate clause puts this country in. It is not a question to my inind how we are to evade the legal result of the contract into which we have entered, but of why, in these negotiations, the government of the day have not put this question beyond the possibility of doubt. We discussed two questions this afternoon, one the provision for the -equipment of $20,000,000 worth of rolling stock. The two or three words, as has been said here to-night, would have put it beyond the possibility of question or doubt. That subject was discussed day after day last session, and hon. gentlemen know the opinion of gentlemen on this side of the House, they obtained opinions from legal gentlemen in Toronto, able gentlemen, although one opinion thus obtained is very difficult to understand at all. Another opinion from that gentleman Inis been produced here in which he omits the vital clause bearing upon the question and never even refers to it. It is not a mere question of what the exact meaning of this clause might prove to be after litigation ; why do not the hon. gentlemen put in a few simple words in order to place the matter beyond question? We urge that they should put in three or four words such as ' acquire and pay for, ' but the hon. gentlemen were so stubborn, if I might use the word, so determined that they would not accept one suggestion from gentlemen on this side of the House, that even when they had the opportunity, when the agreement of last year was thrown over by the Grand Trunk and they were negotiating for new terms, e\en then they would not consider the suggestions we made and would not insert the words to make it more specific. And so here, when they are providing for a lease of property for an unknown period, a lease of $30,000,000 of property, they leave the subject in such a position that they themselves cannot assert here in this House-and I defy any gentleman on the other side to assert it unequivocally-that the construction of that clause is clear and free from doubt. They actually used language which leaves the question so uncertain that I venture to say that the gentleman who prepared the clause would never have used the words that are used here had he for one moment thought of the provision of this seven years without lease. If he had thought of that, if hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches had taken the least trouble to know the terms of the bargain as to the main terms of the lease, they would never have used the words that the interim leases of sections should be on terms not more onerous than the main lease. Why it invited trouble and we can in the inception of this clause what is observable from the beginning to

the end of these negotiations, that everything has been suggested by the Grand Trunk and accepted by the government. Let us see what this is :
Pending the completion of the eastern division by the government, the company-
Mark you, the company.
-shall be entitled to lease from the commissioners-
The company have an option of taking a lease of $30,000,000 worth of property, and cannot be compelled to use it unless they choose to do so. Who inserted these words ? Would they come from any person occupying the position of the government? No, Sir, they come from the person who wanted the option. The company should be entitled to a lease and on terms not more onerous than the main lease. Can it be conceived that a person acting on behalf of the people of Canada would have used these words ' not more onerous than the terms of the main lease,' knowing that by the main lease the first seven years were free and that he would not have used other words than these to protect the country against any possibility that that might mean a free lease for one, two, three, five, six, or seven years? Surely Sir, the hon. gentleman who employed the solicitor to draw a document for him and found that solicitor had put him in this position would say : I want another solicitor to attend to my business hereafter. The people of this country will say : We want another government to attend to our business.
Hear, hear.

That hon. gentlemen may laugh, but the people will not laugh, you may be sure of that. We will take care that the people will have an opportunity to laugh, and when the hon. gentlemen opposite appear on the hustings, we will see on which side of their faces they will laugh.
Oh, oh.
I can only assume from the hilarity of the hon. gentleman from Selkirk and other gentlemen opposite, that they think this is a trifling matter.
You are trifling in most of your discussion.
Not only am I trifling with the subject apparently, but the hon. gentleman thinks it is a trifling subject.
Not at all.

I think it will be regarded otherwise by the people of this country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) knew so little about this Bill that until to-night apparently he did not know that the Bill introduced by the Grand Trunk Pacific last session from first to last was a Bill to run through the city of Winnipeg.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. He said the original project of the Grand Trunk Pacific was to do that.
The original Bill.

The hon. gentleman from Selkirk, knows perfectly well that this House knows nothing about a Bill until it is introduced. We do not know what appears in the Toronto ' Globe, ' or what utterances are made by the Minister of Customs and by two of his colleagues in November, 1902. We look that up now and we find that the hon. gentleman's friends on the other side of the House took up what he called the original project; he had not a word of fault to find with it.
He never said a word.
It is bad enough.

Yes, it is bad enough but we will give you more of it before we get through. The hon. gentleman knows that the only Bill ever presented to this House, the Bill to which the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup) was referring in his speech, was a Bill introduced last session for a road to run through Winnipeg. No other Bill was ever introduced in this House, but the hon. gentleman having made a charge tries to get out of it by saying : Oh. the original proposition that appeared in the Toronto ' Globe ' was the matter that was before the parliament of Canada; that was the original proposition-the original proposition that met with the approval of the Minister of Customs and the approval, I believe, of the Secretary of State and some other gentlemen, and I have no doubt- it met with the approval of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary). We neVer heard of his objection to it. The only proposition that was ever advanced by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company at that time, was the original proposition, which he, himself, says was to go north of Lake Winnipeg. I do not know whether the line was to go north of Lake Winnipeg or not. I know that was the original proposition and the hon. member for Selkirk says that it was to go north of Lake Winnipeg. He seems to have known where it was to have gone. How did he find that out ? We never found him protesting io the press or on the platform against the original proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. The only proposition that was ever brought before the House was to go to Winnipeg. That, we approved of and we take care to say that we approve of it, subject to the condition that there should be terms connected with any subsidy this country should grant, that would protect our own maritime ports and prevent the diversion of traffic to Portland. That is our proposition, that has been our proposition from first to last, and I would like to know where the hon. member for Selkirk finds any objection to our course

in that respect. Now, X say again that we are quite willing to discuss or postpone the discussion of clause 3 of the agreement, but we object to its going forth for one moment, that we think that any doubtful construction of such a clause of so much importance to this country should be made possible, or that we should adopt a clause of that kind when words could be inserted into the Bill which we are discussing which would put the question beyond doubt. We insist that when we come to deal with that section of the Bill, proper provisions shall be inserted so as to ensure that this country shall get a fair return for its money.

Minister of Finance, which certainly interested the committee as well as amazed it, namely, that the Grand Trunk surveyors have been in the field for the last six months, that we are utterly unable to obtain any information from the treasury benches as to where this line will branch off from the main line going south to the head of Lake Superior. Not one of them can give any information, and we must trust to the courtesy of the hon. member for Selkirk for any information that we can get. I am not exactly aware of how many miles eastward of Winnipeg this spur line will deflect, but I will ask the hon. member for Selkirk if he thinks it will be about 300 miles east of Winnipeg ?
About that.

The member for Selkirk admits that at a point 300 miles east of Winnipeg, the line will run south to the head of Lake Superior. He is an understudy of the Minister of the Interior.

No, I cannot assent to that, because the Minister of the Interior won't give us any information, and the member for Selkirk will. The experience of the past is that the bulk of the grain is carried from Superior city or Duluth, to Buffalo, or to Montreal, for export. It is stated to-day in the press that at this early season of the year when insurance rates are very high, charters have been made to carry grain from the head of the lakes to Montreal at five cents per bushel. In the summer months it will be down to three cents, be-
cause vessels now proceeding north with coal receive a better rate than they do later on in the season.
That is not so. The vessels which winter in Duluth and Superior harbours and which can take out 6,000,000 bushels give a smaller rate now than they do latter on in the season.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend in that. The Minister of Justice admitted the other day that last summer wheat was carried from the head of the lakes to Montreal and Quebec for three cents per bushel. At all events, the hon. member (Mr. McCreary), the railway expert of the government, has told us that at a point about 300 miles east of Winnipeg, this spur line to Lake Superior will be built, and he says that of that 300 miles, about 100 miles is prairie country. Well, the experience is that in that prairie section they can construct at the rate of four or five miles per day. so that the first 100 miles will be completed in four or five weeks if the work is pressed with vigour. We may then infer that in about a year, 300 miles of that railway will be built east from Winnipeg. May I ask my hon. friend from Selkirk if he agrees in that inference ?
I am not a railway engineer. Go on with your speech.

We are under an obligation to the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) because he is the only source of inspiration we have on that side of the House. Perhaps he could delve into some past records of the ' Globe,' and if he does we can get some more information from him on the subject. We learn from the statement of the Minister of the Interior, that it is the anticipation of the Grand Trunk Pacific to reach the head of Lake Superior in order to take out the grain and we learn from the First Minister that it is expected by the Grand Trunk Pacific, that they will draw their best paying freight from the province of Ontario. It is therefore in the highest degree probable, that as they have now a line to North Bay, they will build as rapidly as possible the 200 miles or so from North Bay to connect with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and then they will urge that the line on towards Winnipeg, be constructed as soon as possible. I prophesy that long before that line reaches any point north of North Bay, the Grand Trunk Pacific will have a line from the head of Lake Superior to Winnipeg. The Minister of Finance spoke to-day in order to arm himself and his supporters with campaign statements to be used in the maritime provinces. His declaration was, that this whole line was to be constructed at one and the same time, and if the sections are under way from Winnipeg east, at the same time the line will be under construction north of Three Rivers, north of Montreal, down to

Quebec and down to Moncton. But, I noticed that the Minister of Customs did not rise in his place to endorse the statement of the Finance Minister in that respect. I challenge the Minister of Customs to do so now. I do not think he is very warm in this support of the project at the present moment. He worried through some constituencies in Ontario a little while ago, and he found that the reception which the people gave to the Grand Trunk Pacific was not so cordial as the reception it meets from the supporters of the government in this House. During the whole course of this debate, not a single minister from Ontario has stood up to say a word in favour of this proposition, and I do not believe that the Minister of Customs will dare now to endorse the statement of the Finance Minister, that just so soon as this Bill becomes law, contracts will be let at every point from Moncton in the east to Winnipeg in the west. I do not believe the Minister of Customs will endorse that statement, because he is in just the same position as the Postmaster General and the other Ontario ministers. They are arming themselves and their supporters for an Ontario campaign ; but the Minister of Customs is too crafty and careful to stand up and repeat what was said this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, and when the fight comes on next fall, that hon. gentleman and his followers from that province, instead of quoting the Minister of Finance to the effect that the work on the line from one end to the other will be started concurrently, will rather be quoting the report of the Grand Trunk directors to the effect that the construction of the eastern section is a premature work.
Now, Sir, the Minister of Customs has not said a word on this whole matter, and it is notorious that many members from the province of Ontario have demurred to this proposition. I do not believe that the heart of the Minister of Customs is in the work at all. He cannot expect his followers to be enthusiastic at the reception tendered by himself and other ministers to this proposition. The fact of the matter is that in the province of Ontario the ministers are going to rely on what Mr. Ross said in the legislature the other day, that, after all said and done, this Transcontinental Railway was going to be a great feeder for Ontario, as the Grand Trunk Company were going to build a line to North Bay, where it would be brought into communication with the whole province of Ontario. With regard to the lake ports, as all the grain from the Northwest would be carried to the head of Lake Superior, it would be shipped through those different towns which have the advantage of the carrying trade. The fact is, the government intend to play with this question when they go to the electors, and there is no doubt in my mind that this clause is so framed that it will give the Grand Trunk Company practically carte blanche to do what they please with the commissioners. It is patent on the face of the clause that the commissioners are to have a free hand; and if for seven years the company are to have the use of the road free of all charge, then it is quite plain that they can have on the same terms the use of any section of the road that may be completed. When this 300 miles eastward of Winnipeg is built, the Grand Trunk Company may go on with their branch to Port Arthur ; and when that is completed they will have the full user of that portion of the road for practically nothing. I am glad that the Minister of Justice sees that the clause has so many imperfections that he has asked the House to let it stand in the meantime, with the view of probably amending and rectifying it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is certainly an extraordinary spectacle with which we are presented this evening.
