I did not think it was an admission. I thought it was something that every one understood, but I do not think the people of Canada will be dreadfully alarmed when they make a comparison between that $13,000,000 or $14,000,000 in hard cash and the terms which were made for the building of the other transcontinental railway years ago. I think when the people consider that we paid in that case $25,000,000 in hard cash, which is a great deal more than $13,000,000 ; when they consider that in that case we gave 25,000,000 acres of land and that in this case we do not give one acre of land, when they consider that in that case we gave exemptions from taxation and in this case there are no exemptions from taxation, when they consider that in that case we gave over $30,000,000 worth of completed road, when they make a comparison between the two
contracts and when they compare the many millions that we gave away in the case of the other transcontinental railway with the exceedingly modest sum that we are called upon to contribute under this contract to the building of this great transcontinental railway, they will say that the only surprise they have is that we have been able to make such a good bargain. I think that when they compare what has been done this year with what has been done last year they will come to the conclusion that when hon. gentlemen opposite last year said that we had made a poor contract end that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had everything they wanted, they will see that hon. gentlemen have wakened up since to the fact, as the public have, that the contract we put before this House last year was in every respect far and away the best railway contract that had ever been laid before this parliament. The great difficulty was that in our anxiety to protect the public interest we surrounded it with so many checks and guards and so many lines of defence that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had to say to us :	We cannot go on with the work.

If I understand the logic of the hon. gentleman's argument it is, that, having made such a wonderful agreement last year and being in so much worse a position as a result of the negotiations which the hon. gentlemen opposite have carried on with the company, the House had better accept these amendments because if they have another chance of amending the agreement it may be very much worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would like to amend that statement.

Allow me to make the statement for the present. One part of my
hon. friend's argument is this. He said that such dreadful things were done in days gone by

	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say they were dreadful.
Well he said that we had things done in days gone by that were far worse than this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that. I said that this was far better.

The inference which the hon. gentleman wished to have us draw was that the things which are done now are much less dreadful than those which have been done in the past. Therefore the hon. gentleman says :	If I can show you
that some people in days gone by have done some rascally thing, some stupid thing, something beyond the regions of common sense, you have to do nearly that much for the present company. Their argument is something like this :	A man

some years ago stole a sheep ; surely the present government can steal a lamb. What in the name of common sense have we to do with bargains of the past, when we are considering l*y the hard facts of the present day, what the government now propose to do ? Would the Finance Minister in his private transactions, allow any person with whom he was dealing to point out some folly he had committed in his callow youth, as a reason why he should commit the same folly to-day. Surely not. I do not discuss whether what has been done in the past has been good or bad ; folly or wisdom ; but surely we can ask the government to justify their own actions not by the alleged folly of their predecessors, but by the wisdom of what they are proposing to do now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sorry that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) is driven into the position of characterizing the action of his friends of former years, as folly and rascality. I have not done so. On the other hand, I am rather disposed to say that some of us may possibly have been too fearful and too distrustful of events in the days of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. I am rather disposed to give the hon. gentlemen opposite some measure of credit for that great enterprise, and to admit that perhaps some of us were to some extent mistaken. I do not characterize their action of that day as folly and rascality. There was difference of opinion about it, but on the whole that great enterprise turned out better than many expected. If my hon. friend will be glad to have me make that acknowledgment I am disposed to do so, but he himself has been forced to describe the transactions of the men of that day, as folly and rascality.
Nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said nothing of the kind, but that is the only way in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) could apply his argument. I do not say that what was done in the past was folly and rascality. I assume that the money that was paid for that great enterprise was probably wisely paid. At all events, looking back at it, the enterprise has been a great success. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) says that in my own private affairs I would not make comparisons. Well, if I were going to purchase an article that I had not before purchased, I would fiud what some one else had paid for the same article.
About the same date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would make due allowance for the date, but I do not think that the mere change of date would alone account for the vast difference between the obligations which Canada assumed in the former case, and the comparatively moderate obligations, in the proper sense of the Mr. BARKER.
word, which Canada is to assume under this contract.

I quite understand now how many of these clauses have got into the agreement. I presume that if the Grand Trunk Railway had gone to the Minister of Finance and said : such and such a thing was done twenty-five years ago, and you had better do the same thing now ; the hon. gentleman -would at once accept the proposition. If he can only find out that some one, a quarter of a century ago did anything at all extraordinary, that would justify him in doing the same thing to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we are not doing the same thing.
What I said was, that if these things had been done, as the Finance Minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say it.
I did not say they were done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Neither did I.

I did not accuse the hon. gentleman of stealing a lamb, because another gentleman might have stolen a sheep ; I only put it as an illustration, that if these things had been done a quarter of a century ago, that has not the slightest bearing on what he is doing to-day.

The president of the Grand Trunk Railway in his address to his shareholders stated:	That the Grand Trunk
could not at this time expect to receive the same aid as the Canadian Pacific Railway did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Grand Trunk people knew the present government.

No ; they knew the present conditions. Since parliament rose last year the Prime Minister has carefully avoided obtaining any knowledge of the cost of the road, or its location, or the nature of the country through which this eastern section will run, and he consequently looks upon the contract in the same light as he did last year. But the Finance Minister is in a different position. It is his duty to tell us what in his opinion this enterprise will cost the country, assuming that the bonds are sold at three and a quarter per cent, or possibly at three and a half per cent. If at three and a quarter per cent it will run into a good many millions, and if at three and a half per cent it will run into $30,000,000 or $40,000,000. These are figures that cannot be denied. The Minister of Finance assumes that this country has no obligations under this contract, unless in the extraordinary event, as he says, of the whole country going to the dogs. I deny that. I say that this country assumes obligations, and possibly may have to pay large sums of money even though the country be

enormously prosperous, because the government is undertaking to build a road through a territory about which nothing whatever is known from a road standpoint, 'l'he Finance Minister does not contemplate the possibility of the engineers finding difficulties in locating a road of the standard which the country has obligated itself to build. It is possible that a location cannot be found for a road of such a standard. If that be so, and if any one section of this road had to be abandoned, or if its construction had to be postponed for twenty years, then this government is assuming obligations of the most serious character, and though the country may during these twenty years prosper to a degree unthought of, still the country would have to discharge its obligations. The Minister of Finance should place before us fairly and squarely what are the possibilities as to the obligations which the country assumes.

The difficulty seems to be that no one assumes responsibility for the building of this Transcontinental railway. Ordinarily we would expect to have the Minister of Railways here to give answers to reasonable questions, but unfortunately that is not the case in the present instance. This is not a captious criticism, because I believe that we have not altogether departed from the theory of responsible government, and responsible ministers. If there is any reason at all in having cabinet ministers assigned to different departments, surely in a large transaction of this kind-one of the largest Canada has ever engaged in or is likely to engage in for a very long time to come-it would be reasonable to expect that the Minister of Railways, at all events, would be in his seat and would have some information to give us. On the other hand, we have the spectacle of minister after minister, so far as they do speak at all, disclaiming any special knowledge of this matter. The Minister of Justice yesterday was very pronounced in telling us that he was not a railway expert and could not give us the information we desired. The Minister of Finance has taken the same attitude from time to tame, and I think he has borne out in some degree by some of the statements he has made. The right hon. gentleman who introduced the measure explained last night that although at the head of a business government, he is not himself a business man. Thus all those gentlemen who speak at all have disclaimed any possibility of giving us the information we expect on matters of this kind. What is the extraordinary position taken by the Minister of Finance to-night? He says we shall be sur-surprised at the smallness of the figures when he comes to make his calculation of the additional cost involved in this amended contract. I am sure the opposition will not be surprised at the actual
figures when they are correctly made up, whatever the hon. minister's calculations may be. I think the country has a right to expect that not tonight or next week, but at the time the government entered into this transaction with the railway company, when the Minister of Railways was authorized by the cabinet to put his hand to that agreement, and so pledge Canada to this change of contract, the Minister of Finance had ascertained the exact extent of the increased liability the country was incurring. That seems to be a reasonable proposition. Is it not extraordinary that the Minister of Finance has to admit to-night that he cannot give a reasonable approximation of what the increased liability is. I do not think a much more humiliating position could be taken by that hon. gentleman nor by the cabinet as a whole than to be obliged to tell this House, after this matter has taken the form of a definite contract, signed, sealed and delivered-a contract which the government are evidently determined to force through- that thy never made a calculation as to what increased liability is going to be put upon the country by reason of this change. The government have determined to go it blind-first to let the railway company get everything, denying them practically nothing, giving them every concession they ask, and claiming no concession and no benefit for the country, and then come here and tell us that not one member of the government has ever made a calculation to see what increased burdens this change would place upon the people. I do not think I could ask a more complete condemnation of the government. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that we are not so slow as he is in that regard-that we do know something as to the cost.
Since when ?

Since the hon. gentleman came back to the House. I want to tell the Minister of Finance, that, although he says we shall be surprised at the very slight difference, the change will make in the burden assumed by the country, we know that will not turn out to be a fact. If the hon. gentleman had made the calculation and presented it to the House. I might reasonably have some diffidence in controverting his statement. But he has made no calculation, and according to himself he knows nothing about it. Therefore I am at liberty to tell him that we have made a circulation, and unless he says that he regards a difference of four or five millions as a mere bagatelle, it does not agree with what he said he hoped for to-night. I do not think we need resurrect ancient history. There is nothing I suppose, that more condemns a man making an argument, particularly a man of the distinguished ability of the Minister of Finance, nothing that shows more completely



235G
the poverty of the situation in which he stands as regards the support of this contract, than that he has to try to draw a herring across the trail by mentioning the Canadian Pacific Railway in comparison. I think we cannot do better than refer the bon. minister to the argument that was put forward by the hon. Minister of Interior in support of the Bill of last session. That lion, gentleman spoke for probably half an hour to show that this contract would be profitable to both parties, that there was no use of talkng about it being a failure, that it was of a character that must secure the success of the company as well as advantage to the government and the country. He pointed out the difference between the conditions under which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company had to build their line and the conditions under which this company are undertaking the transcontinental railway. He emphasized the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway had gone through the poorest part of the country, whilst this railway bad the very pick and choice of that great western portion of Canada in which to build. He also pointed out the almost insuperable difficulties that were met by the Canadian Pacific Railway at that day, as contrasted with the facilities with which this company will obtain its supplies. No better argument probably could be submitted in answer to the hon. Finance Minister than the argument of his own colleague. The Minister of the Interior completely refutes, if reputation is necessary, the argument based on this comparison by the Minister of Finance. But even if the Canadian Pacific Railway had never been mentioned, by the Minister of the Interior, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will certainly receive no support and no consolation from" the people in the country by asking that a contrast be made between the conditions under which the Canadian Pacific Railway was built and the condition under which this line is to be built.
Any one knows that the conditions to-day are entirely different from what they were when the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was undertaken. Then the Northwest was a great lone land and an unknown land, in the possibilities of which the Conservative party in this country alone had faith. And it is plain that what would be a reasonable estimate in those days for the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway could serve as no justification whatever for the entering into this extraordinary contract by this government. When we try to find out what this contract ready implies, we can find no one on the government benches capable of giving any accurate information. Not one of them apparently has made the study of it a specialty, and the result is we have from the various ministers who have spoken on this question the most loose, contradictory and unreliable statements. We certainly are entitled to expect Mr. LENNOX.
from the Minister of Finance a careful estimate of the additional burden which the section we are now discussing will put upon the people, but that hon. gentleman is evidently not in a position to relieve the public mind on that point. I submit, we Should never have been asked to consider these important amendments without previously having had from the Minister of Finance an accurate estimate of the increased liability which the country is thereby assuming. But instead we find ministers making most general, inconclusive and uncertain statements. Who has charge of this matter ? Certainly the Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson) has l'.ot. The Minister of Justice disclaims having anything more to do with it than to pronounce on its legal questions. The right hon. gentleman who introduced the measure, and who has more at stake in it than anybody else, because his future fame depends upon its success, has been so uncertain in the statements he has made from time to time, that we cannot place reliance on them. Take for instance, what he said in connection with the amendment we are now considering. On the 5th of April, when introducing these amendments, and apologizing for them, he said :
The next section is more important. It relates to the assistance to be given by the government for the construction of the western division. These provisions of the new contract are embraced in sections 4 and 5.
If this is a section of special importance, we certainly have the right to expect that the information of the right hon. gentleman regarding it would be accurate. What does he say ? After quoting the words of the section-and I must say we would have had much more accurate information if he had stopped there and not gone on to give his own interpretation, he proceeded to say :
The government would not accept either of these propositions, but the proposition which was finally adopted is embodied in the section I have just read, and is to this effect. First of all the restrictions as to the liability of the government guarantee in the mountain section is removed. In the original contract the government guarantee was limited to $30,000 per mile on the mountain section, but now we undertake to guarantee 75 per cent of the cost of construction, whatever it may be, without any restriction. Then we undertake also to implement the proceeds of the sales of the bonds, so as to make the amount actually going into the construction, 75 per cent of the total cost of construction. This is to be done on conditions further to be agreed upon between the government and the country.
He gave tbe House to understand, then, that this undertaking to implement tbe proceeds of the sale of the bonds, so as to obtain their face value, applies only to the mountain section. But that is not the case. The fact is that this undertaking extends to the prairie as well as to the mouri-

laiu section. This is a very material difference. It might be said, possibly, that there was something vague about it, that the right hon. gentleman was only speaking of the mountain section, but a little careful attention will show that that could not have been the case, because he said :
Then we undertake also to implement the proceeds of the sale of the bonds, so as to make the amount actually going into the construction, 75 per cent of the total cost of construction.
We do not undertake, as regards the prairie section, to guarantee 75 per cent of the cost, whatever that may be, but we only undertake to guarantee an amount not exceeding $13,000 per mile. Beyond that limit our guarantee does not go, either in the new or the old contract, so that when we find the right hon. gentleman saying, when speaking of the mountain section, that we are to implement the proceeds of the bonds as regards the 75 per cent guarantee, we know conclusively that ififei intended to confine ^thot observation to the mountain section. What does this show? It does not show of course, that the right ho ill gentleman intended to mislead the House or the country-I would not for a moment say anything of the kind-but what 1 do say is that from first to last, whoever has come forward as the exponent of the position of the government, has been hazy, and none more so than the right hon. gentleman, I cannot for one moment imagine that the right hon. gentleman intended to mislead anybody, and therefore I am forced to the conclusion that he did not understand the matter with which he was dealing.

I am one of those referred to as having made use of the estimates of the cost to this country of the road which arc to be found in the speeches delivered at the introduction of this Bill last year. I no doubt' have done so. But it is not because I accepted these estimates as accurate. On the contrary I pointed out that when the Prime Minister estimated the cost to the country, during the period the Grand Trunk Pacific would have a lease of the road, at $13,000,000. there was not one of his followers' who did not quote that estimate as being the total cost to this country of the construction of the road.
Therefore, if it could be misunderstood by the followers of the Prime Minister in this House how very misleading it could be, and was calculated to be, in the country at large! The Finance Minister referred to that estimate, and, taking it as correct said that it could be met by an arrangement with a trust company for the present payment of some $8,000,000-1 think it was $8,000,000; certainly not more than $9,000,000. The deposit of this sum of money, he said, would suffice to pay the $13,000,000 of the Prime 754
Minister's estimate as the payments of which it was made up came due. if members of the House sitting behind the government could misunderstand the meaning, if they could believe that this was the total cost to Canada, how much more were the people at large likely to be misled by calculations of this kind ? We know now what they meant. There is no attempt to dispute that the total obligation for the building of the road is enormously larger than $9,000,000 or $13,000,000. These obligations will be not less than $150,000,000. If their railway expert, Hon. Mr. Blair, were making the calculation to-day as he made it last year, and adding the increased obligation of this amended contract to the $139,000,000 of his estimate of that time ; he could not calculate the obligation at less than about $150,000,000. And, to-night, we find hon. gentlemen opposite driven from every defence of this contract by the fair, sound and businesslike criticism, and with nothing left to fall back upon except to say : But what did you do with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway contract some thirty years ago ? When that is their only defence, it shows what a hopeless position they are in. We are not here to discuss what was done thirty years ago. The conditions then and the conditions now are so totally different that comparison is impossible. The point to be considered now is what conclusion reasonable business men should arrive at with regard to the contract before us. It is quite evident to this House, and must be evident to the country at large, that the government have been unfairly matched-matched with men who are far their superiors in business acumen. It may be said to the credit of the chief manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and his co-directors that they have made an excellent bargain in the interest of their company. I do not know that the Finance Minister has made any attempt so far this session to explain why he was so emphatic in saying that if the Grand Trunk should attempt to get out of its obligations this contract was so firmly and strictly made that it would hold them tight. He said they could not get out of it, for instance, with reference to the $25,000,000 of stock- they could not dispose of a single dollar's worth of it-where is the hon. gentleman on that question to-night. He has not a word to say in defence of his position. It is all gone to the winds along with every guarantee and proviso that was inserted in the original contract in the interest of the people of Canada. All abandoned and not a word to be said in their defence.

I shall not occupy the attention of the House at any length. The minister (Mr. Fielding) seemed to think that I had misrepresented what he said, and as I have no desire to misrepresent the hon. gentleman or any other member of this House, I would take the liberty of remind-

ing him of his exact words, as they appear in the revised ' Hansard ' :
My toon, friend the Prime Minister in the course of his speech said that we could meet the responsibilities of this contract by setting aside the present year's surplus which is roundly stated at $13,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite have thought that was a rash statement. I am convinced that the figures I shall be able to give to the House will show that my hon. friend's statement is substantially correct.
And then he recited the various items to make up his total of $11,512,000. So, I do not think I misrepresented it very much. Speaking of the hybrid contract, part of the line to be owned by the government and part by the company, one speaker, the exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) estimated the obligation at $130,000,000 or $140,000,000, and, in answer to this the Minister of Finance said that less than $8,000,000 would meet the responsibility of the contract. I am not surprised that the people thought that this was all it would cost the country to have that road built.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) is too good a lawyer not to know the weakness of reading a portion of a statement like that. He will see that the whole argument was based upon an actual calculation of what would be the country's share of expense on the assumption that the Grand Trunk would fulfil its obligation, and I am sure that he so understood it.
Progress reported.

Monday, May 2, 1904.
